articleTitle: Gadgets
abstract: Gadgets that let you speak 74 languages, get ready for summer, display doodles and finally have a proper hands-free digital assistant in the car.

articleTitle: Gadgets: High-tech gifts for lovers of genealogy, weather, music and astronomy, plus the ultimate party camera
Gadgets: Get out and about with high-tech running, audio and coffee-making gear, or stay at home and wallow in arcade game nostalgia
Gadgets forkids
Formula E: The journey so far
abstract: THE 2019/20 FORMULA E season is just around the corner, with 24 drivers and 12 teams from across the world battling it out for the championship title in the highest class competition for electric open-wheel racing.

articleTitle: Planet ocean: The last frontier: With most of the ocean seabed unmapped, earth's last frontier of terrestrial discovery has become a focus of activity for explorers, scientists, cartographers and environmentalists
abstract: ASK ANY EXPLORER what there is left to explore and, apart from the vast cosmos about which we know virtually nothing, the most frequent answer will be “the ocean depths”. This is because, while the planet's dry surface has been mapped down to the last metre, we know very little about the topography of the bottom of our oceans. Water covers 70 per cent of the globe and yet, by some estimates, only 10 per cent of the ocean floor has been explored to a significant degree. The race is now on to map the entire seabed by the end of the next decade.

articleTitle: A real addiction? Tech addiction is the scourge of the modern age — or is it? In fact, is tech addictive at all?
abstract: DOES TECHNOLOGY addiction really exist? And is it damaging us? Ask any parent whose adolescent child is chained to their device or obsessed by gaming into the small hours — and they'll agree. So too does the World Health Organization (WHO), which controversially classified “gaming disorder” as a disease in 2018.

articleTitle: Cycling with the current: Electric bikes could be set to make a big impact — not just on the cycling community but on society as a whole
abstract: THERE HAS ALWAYS been a bias against the e-bike — that feeling that it is cheating, a stigma of laziness. But as the cycling boom continues not just in the UK but across Europe, the role of the e-bike is not only gaining acceptance, it is now moving to centre stage. While there are a host of reasons that an e-bike may suit individual needs, the key point is that they make mobility more accessible to more people.

articleTitle: Can big data help curb the opioid crisis?
abstract: THE OPIOID CRISIS CLAIMS over a hundred lives every day in the US alone. Medically known as the Opioid Use Disorder (OUD), the crisis that's taken the form of an epidemic impacts everyone across economic barriers and social strata. Dr Meera Kanhouwa describes how an anaesthesiologist friend recently committed suicide on Mother's Day: "If a physician who has access to care feels so disconsolate, what are we missing?" With over two decades of working in emergency rooms (ERs) across the US, Kanhouwa wishes she knew who was at risk: "When two people walk into my ER — same age and same back pain — who is going to be an opioid addict, or who is at risk of opioid addiction? And who has resilience? Anything I know in my gut is not a data-driven approach."

articleTitle: Reel to reel rebirth: Analogue tape almost disappeared as the world went digital in the 1980s. But it's back for a second pass
abstract: FRANKIE GOES TO Hollywood's 1984 Cold War anthem ‘Two Tribes’ was an unusual summer hit with its worries over nuclear annihilation. But it rose quickly after release and lingered at the top of the charts for two months. Although barely remembered today musically, the single seemed to point the way to the future.

articleTitle: True grit
abstract: GRAPHENE WAS ORIGINALLY identified for use as a transistor in computing but, as researchers catalogued its properties, it became clear that it could be used for many other applications.

articleTitle: Gadgets
abstract: Retro styling and the latest technology combine to make this premium electric bike badass. At its heart is a bespoke, brushless, three-phase DC motor and 48V battery pack. There's optional solar charging and regenerative braking: using the motor coils in reverse to charge the batteries. rayvoltbike.co.uk

articleTitle: Echoes of an extreme past: On the 80th anniversary of the beginning of the second world war, do we need to learn from history about how to deal with extremists who use communications technology to spread their hate?
abstract: AT 11:15 AM on 3 September 1939, Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain told the British people that the nation was at war with Germany. The Nazi regime had sent a military force into Poland two days earlier and had not responded to the withdrawal demand from the British and French.

articleTitle: How to be remembered like da Vinci
abstract: AT A TIME WHEN technology innovation moves more quickly than regulation and research, how can someone born before the European discovery of the Americas still be of use to modern science? Leonardo da Vinci's concepts have not merely withstood the test of time, but thrive in today's academic circles, and his inventions are cited to add value to reports of scientific advances.

articleTitle: Bizarre tech: Welcome to Bizarre Tech, and another instalment of weird stuff. This time, we have a touchy bear, anti-stink-six-day-wear socks, and a big ol'rubbing chair
abstract: The makers of this bear wrote a paper that highlighted how humans have a fundamental need to be connected to others. Remote touch can potentially be used in various ways, from social interaction to therapeutic use.

articleTitle: The teardown: Nintendo Game Boy: Inside the original 8-bit handheld console on its 30th anniversary
abstract: THIS YEAR MARKS the 30th anniversary of the launch of Nintendo's original Game Boy, though it did not make its way to Europe until 1990. At around £70 (about twice that in today's prices), it put high technology in your pocket at a cost mobile phones were still some way from matching. And it saw off other contemporary entries in the handheld space, including Apple's Newton.

articleTitle: Improbable machines
abstract: ONE REASON WHY Leonardo da Vinci's legacy has endured so long lies in his apparent willingness to embrace the future. His paintings were created at a time when art was changing stylistically into forms that would endure for centuries. And he was a prolific inventor and conceptualist with ambitious ideas as to what his inventions could ultimately achieve.

articleTitle: Could we avert a major asteroid strike? Earth's atmosphere is regularly peppered by asteroids, most of which do little harm. however, once every few million years something much bigger comes along, putting life on Earth at risk. could we stop one?
abstract: ON THE MORNING of 15 February 2013, just as people were starting work, a blinding light tore across the winter skies of south-western Russia. An explosion equivalent to 440,000 tonnes of TNT generated a shockwave that blew out windows and damaged buildings over an area of 200 square miles. The house-size Chelyabinsk asteroid, which flared 14 miles above ground, left 1,600 people with injuries, mainly caused by broken glass.

articleTitle: New crypto on the block: There's a new cryptocurrency in town, but the long-rumoured stablecoin Libra will have to overcome some major obstacles to become an investible asset
abstract: FACEBOOK's PROPOSED launch of a new cryptocurrency, Libra, has certainly stirred up some interest. The initiative is backed by a 28-strong consortium, the Libra Association, based in Switzerland. Facebook subsidiary Calibra has a leading role, and other key participants that have been announced include Visa, MasterCard, PayPal, Lyft, Uber, Vodafone Group and many others across blockchain, telecommunications, payments and venture capital firms, as well as non-profits.

articleTitle: Da Vinci's new Milan
abstract: ‘RENAISSANCE MEN’ had been dreaming about the perfect cityscape before Leonardo da Vinci. The idea of using rules and angles to create a zone of majestic order appealed to many a polymath of the time, artist and philosopher Leon Battista Alberti among them.

articleTitle: Solving crimes with geology
abstract: TWENTY-TWO SERIES and 200 episodes of the BBC CSI drama ‘Silent Witness’ testifies to the enduring appeal of forensics in television. Real CSI (crime scene investigation) is somewhat different — less intuitive, more scientific, but just as fascinating, perhaps more so.

articleTitle: Could we start from scratch?
abstract: ARMAGEDDON OR the apocalypse, the end of the world as we know it. Whatever the disaster, whatever the reason, you've awakened on the technology equivalent of Robinson Crusoe's desert island. And just as the shipwreck victim had to start from first principles — building shelter, finding food, finding his way around — so do you.

articleTitle: State of independence: Is America's tech policy, rather than hampering semiconductor innovation in China, actually boosting it?
abstract: CHINA's LONG-STANDING bid for technological independence, including its semiconductor ambitions, are again climbing the global agenda. In the West, the Trump administration's clampdown in August on Huawei's access to US technology highlights — and reflects — concerns about China's goals as stated in programmes like Made in China 2025.

articleTitle: Awareness through art
abstract: "THE BOOK ‘Brave New World’ really influenced me when I was a youngster," says Dr Jasmine Pradissitto as she takes me on a tour of her south London studio. "I can see that we're going down that road," she adds, referring to a world more hopeful and expressing how humans, in years to come, have the ability to evolve above the dystopian views highlighted in the 1932 novel.

articleTitle: Energy networks: Getting hotter: Are heat networks about to take off in the UK?
abstract: YOU MIGHT OBSESS about turning the lights off but, the truth is, electricity only makes up a tiny part of your carbon footprint. In fact, around 80 per cent of UK home energy use comes from heating space and water, and most of that is generated by individual gas boilers sitting in dusty cupboards. While that's clearly an improvement on burning coal, it's still a fairly inefficient system, dependent on fossil fuels, that needs to be tackled to cut the nation's carbon footprint.

articleTitle: Rebooting moon travel: It has been 50 years since Neil Armstrong made exploration history with that first of many boot-prints on the Moon and since 1972, when the last of the 12 Moonwalkers left the surface of our nearest planetary body no-one has returned. Is it time to put those lunar boots back on?
abstract: ONE DICTIONARY DEFINITION of exploration is “an organised trip into unfamiliar regions, especially for scientific purposes”. The exploration of space certainly fits the definition in terms of unfamiliar regions, but the ‘trip’ is often made by automated, rather than manned, vehicles for cost and safety reasons. To many in the space fraternity this is half-hearted exploration, because it lacks the essential essence of exploration as an intrinsic human activity; although it references a science-fiction cliché, they would prefer “to boldly go where no-one has gone before”.

articleTitle: An ethical balancing act
abstract: POLICE FORCES ACROSS England and Wales are poised to develop AI models to assess reoffending risk for convicted offenders. Bearing the brunt of a wave of criticism, partly due to its laudable efforts to be more transparent than other forces, is West Midlands Police (WMP). It is currently building such a system and expects it to kick off later in the year — but only if it can accommodate the concerns of its ethics committee. While WMP points out that the current accuracy rate of 75 per cent is a vast improvement on previous figures, one key concern is that the new model could wrongly label innocent ex-offenders as ‘harmful’.

articleTitle: Gadgets
abstract: Technology will make light work of your lawn, your cooking, even your gnashers.

articleTitle: A change in computing
abstract: THE CHANCES ARE high that most people you know have never heard of skyrmions. This is natural, because they are rather murky products of quantum field theory that act like particles without actually being particles. So far so obscure. Skyrmions, however, may soon be as well known as silicon chips. That's because they have the potential to change the face of computing, revolutionising the fields of data storage, information processing and artificial intelligence.

articleTitle: Plastic-free produce
abstract: THE STORE, called Re:Store, only opened this February and was created by founder Megan Adams, who is urging Londoners to reduce plastic use.

articleTitle: To boldly go the history of space exploration: With further wonders of the universe still untouched, we remember the groundbreaking space missions of the past and discover how they are helping to unlock the secrets of our solar system today
abstract: AS NASA CALLED out in vain to the Dawn spacecraft on All Saint's Day last year, the space world held its breath. After more than a decade venturing into orbits unknown, capturing never-before-seen images and making discoveries that touch the far reaches of our Solar System, Dawn's fuel had finally run out. Despite its muted end, the mission was an overwhelming scientific success, not merely because it represented an apex. Dawn wasn't just 11 years in the making — the precision needed, the advanced sensors and the way its development transcended disciplines and countries was the culmination of centuries of technological advances, while the mission lived up to its name by ushering in a new dawn of space exploration.

articleTitle: Gadgets
abstract: Smoothies with added science. A battery powered pump sucks out the air before blending, so that your drink oxidises much less. This should retain nutrients, as well as colour and flavour, for longer.

articleTitle: Seven upstarts of upcycling: Today's dominant production model creates vast amounts of waste. However, engineers and designers are finding increasingly imaginative ways to repurpose industrial by-products into valuable new materials
abstract: WHAT's NOT TO like about the idea of a ‘circular economy’? Unlike our current economic model, where products follow a straight line from factory to consumer to landfill, a circular economy would see products designed with a view to being re-used, and new materials would be made from exhausted goods.

articleTitle: How to pay women engineers more
abstract: LATEST FIGURES, released in April, show that the gender pay gap is actually growing in 45 per cent of the UK's biggest firms.

articleTitle: Gadgets: Winter sports, TV, family entertainment, fitness, even your morning coffee improved thanks to innovation
The advantage of thinking differently
abstract: "I DIDN'T GET diagnosed until quite late on," says James Neely, IT consultant. "I was working and it had got quite stressful. We'd moved office a few times and the journey got longer. We got more condensed and it was a lot noisier and the journey wasn't as manageable anymore, until the point when I actually ended up going off with clinical depression and anxiety. Then out of the treatment for that, it was realised I was autistic.

articleTitle: Your game or mine? Dual-usestadium gives NFL a London base
abstract: FIVE DAYS AFTER Tottenham Hotspur lost 7-2, at home to Bayern Munich in the Champions League, the Chicago Bears and Oakland Raiders came to the new Spurs stadium to play an NFL (American football) match. The following Sunday so did the Carolina Panthers and the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.

articleTitle: Designed to survive: If you want to win the Vendée Globe, the single-handed, non-stop race around the world, then winning is not your first challenge. Your first challenge is to survive
abstract: IT's THE ULTIMATE sailing challenge. The Vendée Globe demands sailors circumnavigate the globe, single-handed, non-stop and unsupported. The main event itself doesn't set sail until November 2020, but it is the conclusion of a four-year cycle in the sport that is currently ramping up with its main warm-up event, the Transat Jacques Vabre. This is the event that, in many cases, represents a first look at the yachts that will contend for the main prize next year.

articleTitle: Artificial intelligence energy: AI — energy's untapped resource: Artificial intelligence and robotics look set to transform the nature of work in the energy industry, shifting the focus away from on-site fault-finding to higher-skilled jobs in control centres
abstract: THE ARRIVAL OF the Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) has led to the collection and transmission of vast amounts of new and complex data, in the energy sector just as elsewhere. However, this huge inflow of data, gathered via connected devices such as sensors placed along pipelines in oil and gas fields and power plants, needs to be processed, analysed and interpreted if it is to be useful.

articleTitle: Gadgets: Supercharge your phone, wallet and watch. Meanwhile rechargeable tech is transforming pressure washers as well as vacuum cleaners
Too old to be an engineer?
abstract: TRY TO IMAGINE someone working in the tech industry and you'll visualise a man in his late 20s playing ping-pong and wearing designer jeans and sneakers. You wouldn't be wrong. The average age of a Google employee is 29. As Facebook's founder Mark Zuckerberg, now the ripe age of 35, famously said: "Young people are just smarter"

articleTitle: AI-powered therapy sets minds at rest
abstract: IT MADE HEADLINE news when the leader of the UK's biggest relationship support charity revealed the organisation was considering the possibility of deploying chatbots using artificial intelligence (AI) for live chat counselling services. The chief executive of Relate, Aidan Jones, told an interviewer that he was looking at the potential of "non-human intervention" in 2019 to assist his 1,500 online counsellors, as they were becoming stretched by demands made on the service.

articleTitle: The ages of materials
abstract: EVEN SINCE WE FIRST picked up a rock to crack open a nut or sharpened a stick to spear a fish or used a flint to create a spark to light a fire, we've been using tools. Ever since we first plaited long grasses to make a rope with which to lash together a few branches to make shelter, we've been creating buildings. From the moment we realised that some rocks split open to produce sharp edges, we've developed weapons.

articleTitle: Take to the skies: After decades of promises, the vision of ‘flying cars’ is finally getting close to commercial reality. But what projects are currently in the works?
abstract: THE 1982 CULT sci-fi classic ‘Blade Runner’ envisioned a future full of LED umbrellas, robots (or ‘replicants’) indistinguishable from human beings, and, most notably, flying cars. This world created by director Ridley Scott was set in Los Angeles in 2019.

articleTitle: Deep-space observatory prepares for life-off
abstract: WHEN THE WORLD's most powerful telescope eventually launches, space scientists will hold their breath. Equipped with the most delicate and sensitive optics ever built, the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) — a launch that has been delayed by 14 years and is roughly ten times over budget — will probe deeper and further back into space than ever before: revealing first light, the start of the universe, the birth of stars, and possibly the origins of life.

articleTitle: Through the looking glass
abstract: IMAGINE LOOKING DOWN at your body and discovering you're a different gender or race. You're in someone's virtual shoes, experiencing the world as he or she, or even they, sees it — joy, fear, prejudice, and how others perceive you.

articleTitle: Algorithms for anoraks
abstract: CRICKET FANS of yesteryear diligently filled in their scorecards and referred to the sports pages or their Wisden Almanac if they needed to know something about the match or one of the players. These days, a new generation of fans use their smartphones to access and understand cricket's finer points.

articleTitle: 40 years of the four-track: How TEAC created the Portastudio legend
abstract: EVER SINCE THE first musicians beat out a rhythm on a hollow log, artists have dreamed of recording their ideas for posterity. Unfortunately, creative types were limited by the technology available to them.

articleTitle: The teardown apple iPad 7: Apple has upgraded its basic tablet in a Trumpian yet canny way
abstract: THE SEVENTH-GENERATION standard iPad from Apple has arrived. The most significant thing about its teardown is how little the company has done. While that might disappoint you from an engineering perspective, there is a bigger story to think about.

articleTitle: Brain-reading tech: Lets users control devices through thought alone
abstract: THE IDEA OF controlling technology just by thinking about what you want to do, without the need for any physical interaction, is a long-standing one that's been a frequent fixture in science fiction's vision of what life will be like in the future.

articleTitle: Breathe in a new breed: We meet six young innovators who are leading the way in using their skills and talent to shape the future of technology
abstract: AMERICA'S MICROSOFT, Google, Apple, Facebook and Amazon, as well as China's Alibaba and Tencent, have touched the lives of countless millions. Hard on the heels of these titans of the tech world — which were virtually unheard of just three decades ago — are Uber, WeWork and Airbnb. These companies offer services from ride-hailing to office accommodation, and are growing fast thanks to cloud computing, smartphones, social media, low interest rates and huge customer bases.

articleTitle: AI passes go — where next? China has announced ambitious plans to lead the world in artificial intelligence, but it will have to overcome some major obstacles to achieve that. How realistic are its aspirations?
abstract: IN JULY 2017, China published its Next Generation AI Development Plan. As analysts such as Jeff Ding of Oxford University point out, it was not a green-field programme. It rather sought to gather and focus a diverse set of existing initiatives in response to what local academics called a ‘Sputnik moment’: the 2016 defeat of the world's best Go player, Lee Sedol, by a Google-owned AI.

articleTitle: Gadgets
abstract: This cycle helmet folds away when not in use but, even more impressively, it protects your bonce time and time again. It's made from a new polymer that's less brittle than EPS. In impact tests, it survives more than 80 hits where a traditional helmet fails after just two.

articleTitle: 7 top jobs for the future: Automation and AI technology are set to change the workplace. But this is not simply the death knell for engineering jobs that the doomsayers predict. It will also lead to the creation of a whole new set of tasks that can only be done by humans. Here are some of the posts we all might be applying for in the future
abstract: FROM THE ROBOTIC mechanics, soldiers, doctors and — most famously — translators in ‘Star Wars’, to the spider-like police spies in ‘The Minority Report’, dystopian films and books have long warned that robots will take our jobs. But fact is becoming stranger than fiction in the 21st century, with experts warning we may be twiddling our non-metallic thumbs within decades thanks to strides in automation and AI technologies.

articleTitle: TheTeardown: Google pixel 3a smartphone
abstract: NOT ALL MID-RANGE smartphones are the same. At £399, the Google Pixel 3a does not feel that mid-range at all, until you bear in mind that it is a more ‘affordable’ addition to the range than the £739 Pixel 3. It is still a hefty-looking price tag, though, when compared to the highly functional and, for most users, satisfactory handsets offered at between £200 and £250 by brands such as Motorola and Xiaomi.

articleTitle: Putting perfection: The BMW PGA Championship is the flagship event on golf's European tour. As this year's event gets under way at Wentworth, golfers will expect the Surrey course to be in tip-top condition. We look at the technology used to achieve perfection
abstract: WENTWORTH HAS a glittering past for golfing drama, having been the venue for both the World Matchplay and the PGA Championship. Winners across the two competitions include the sport's most iconic figures — Jack Niclaus, Arnold Palmer, Greg Norman, Tom Watson, Seve Ballesteros, Nick Faldo and many, many more. This year the 2019 BMW PGA Championship has switched from the spring to September to accommodate the US tour schedule.

articleTitle: Digital doomsday: The threat of cyber attack hangs over all of us, but how big could it get? Could hackers bring society to a standstill — a digital Armageddon?
abstract: HUNDREDS OF thousands of cyber attacks are launched against critical energy, utility, banking, transport and healthcare systems every year, but could they ever bring the world's digital systems to their knees simultaneously to cause economic, social and political chaos on a truly global scale?

articleTitle: Fending off disaster
abstract: THE FOUR HORSEMEN of the apocalypse may have been the equine-borne harbingers of doom in ancient revelations but in today's global threat landscape, we are more likely to hear of disaster from our smartphones than anything as dramatic as alarming horse riders in billowing robes.

articleTitle: Space: ‘The new AI frontier’?
abstract: IN RECENT YEARS, the concept of artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged from the annals of science fiction into everyday life, as society grapples with a range of technological issues from cyber security to driverless cars. Along with other terms, such as machine learning, neural networks and ‘the Turing test’, AI has become a contemporary media buzzword in both fact and fiction — despite a general lack of understanding of what AI really means to the average citizen of Earth.

articleTitle: All the all-round geniuses
abstract: MANY MAJOR discoveries have been made repeatedly by different inventors working without knowledge of each other's research. Newton and Leibniz invented calculus, Wallace and Darwin found the theory of natural selection at the same time, and Alexander Graham Bell put in a patent for the telephone on the same day as Elisha Gray. These are the quite well-known cases.

articleTitle: Clinging to life: If the worst happens, how can we survive?
abstract: IF YOU WANT TO live through Armageddon, talk to a space scientist. From understanding the microbes that thrive in extreme environments to studying past sustainability crises on Earth and other planets, these researchers are piecing together life in the universe to understand how to survive today.

articleTitle: How to hack into the IOT: An E&T investigation carried out with leading cyber-threat experts reveals how simple it is to hack web-connected Internet of Things (IoT) devices and explores the implications for consumers and critical infrastructure in the UK
abstract: THE UBIQUITOUSNESS of IoT devices — often dubbed “internet of sh..t”, according to one expert interviewed at InfoSecurity, the annual cyber-security conference held in London — means hackers have a conformable way into systems and our private lives. Even more worryingly, it also means they have potential access to the critical infrastructure systems that run our daily lives.

articleTitle: EU takes airbus as the model for post-Brexit technology leadership: The European Union has some ambitious plans for the next decade, from which the post-Brexit UK could find itself excluded. Maros Sefcovic, the EU official tasked with ‘foresight’, tells E&T that batteries, artificial intelligence and 5G are all on the radar
abstract: IT IS ‘ALL CHANGE’ in Brussels, where the EU institutions are in the middle of their five-yearly reshuffle. When the new European Commission starts work on 1 November, Slovakian diplomat Maros Sefcovic will take on duties that include overseeing a department charged with ‘strategic foresight’ — i.e. identifying long-term trends that are likely to disrupt society, the economy and technology. The plan is simple: pick the ones the EU has the best chance to dominate and invest big in them.

articleTitle: Eyes in the sky protect forests from ‘death by chocolate’: Our consumption of chocolate drives deforestation in many parts of Africa. Researchers are now exploring how satellite data could help farmers cultivate the raw material, cocoa, more sustainably
abstract: SOME PEOPLE SWEAR it calms their nerves; others simply enjoy its rich unique flavour. Chocolate is a sweet treat popular across generations and, in its dark low-sugar variety, sought after even by health-conscious foodies. Demand for chocolate is rising globally, with Europe being the biggest consumer. In the UK, an average person consumes about 7kg of it per year. What chocolate lovers don't realise is that their sweet tooth is contributing to the destruction of rainforests in many parts of Africa.

articleTitle: Lingering austerity: Stymies local carbon cutting efforts
abstract: WHAT IS THE quickest way to clamp down on carbon emissions? The global financial crisis, says Mags Tingey, who studies local government low-carbon strategies as part of the Heat and the City research group at the University of Edinburgh. "There is a clear correlation between the impact of the financial crisis and emissions," she says. This theory held true while waning energy demand in 2008 and 2009 caused emissions to dive universally. But could we find solutions that work just as decisively at a local level — and without the eventual turmoil?

articleTitle: Honey, I shrunk everything!
abstract: IF YOU'VE EVER seen a nappy drenched in water — or other less palatable fluids — you'll know that they can expand quite a lot. What you might not know is that the same material can now be used, in reverse, to shrink objects to nano-scales. In fact, nappies might be about to blow the world of nano-technology wide open.

articleTitle: Apollo and US: Nasa's lunar-landing mission in July 1969 pioneered a crucial new relationship between humans and machines
abstract: NO ONE WHO grew up dreaming of being an astronaut will have imagined it might involve merely being some anonymous component of a complex feedback system. That's not what being an astronaut is. Being an astronaut is being in the driving seat, right? Blast-off. Landing the Eagle. Re-entry. Heroics. But, believe it or not, the test pilots and military aviators selected to become Nasa's first astronauts had a fight on their hands to retain that status.

articleTitle: Under the ICE: The polar expedition: Antarctica's ice caps conceal a pristine and mysterious world. Recent expeditions have started to unveil the secrets of the glacial lakes that lie beneath, while carefully avoiding contamination
abstract: IT IS NO exaggeration to say that we know more about the surface of Mars than we do about Antarctica's subglacial environments, but that is changing thanks to recent expeditions that have penetrated a lost world beneath the ice sheet.

articleTitle: Skills shortage? The answers female
abstract: ONE OF THE WORLD'S most powerful people, German Chancellor with a doctorate in quantum chemistry, Angela Merkel once said that "one swallow does not a summer make": she meant that her achievement did not signify the end of the battle to help more women to fulfill their potential.

articleTitle: Unexpected ways factories are saving energy
abstract: GREEN-MINDED companies are using traditional energy-generation methods such as solar power and wind turbines to good effect. However, some are turning to apparently quirkier solutions that focus on conservation of energy.

articleTitle: Fashion crisis: A need for change
abstract: WOULD YOU BUY a dress for $9,500 (£7,500), even if it was the most beautiful garment you've ever seen? And what if it didn't even exist? If the gossamer-thin, translucent fabric was simply a computer file – albeit unique?

articleTitle: The whole story of& Exploration: Part one: Brave new world part two: Age of instruments part three: Digital earth and beyond: Map-making goes back to the dawn of exploration, but the first systematic approaches only became possible with the arrival of time-keeping technology
abstract: Although humankind's migration out of the African continent started some two million years ago, this gradual spread through tribal relocation across the globe isn't exploration in modern terms. We tend now to think of the purpose of exploration in economic, geopolitical and resource availability terms. The way we have sought to make that easier, notes Eugene Rae, expert in the history of exploration instrumentation and artefacts at Royal Geographical Society, “is to have better technology”.

articleTitle: Pump it up!: Water jets are no longer used just for thrill-seeking jet-skiers. Now larger boats in a variety of applications are using the technology for propulsion — so what's powering the trend?
abstract: THE FIRST THING that may come to mind when you think of water-jet propulsion is the jet skis that are popular with holiday-goers and adrenaline junkies. Traditionally the system has been used in small vessels such as these and the jetboats used by coastguards, the navy and others. Since 2000, however, this technology has increasingly been used by larger vessels such as military ships and ferries. But what makes water jets (also called pump jets) appeal more to operators in these fields than traditional propellers?

articleTitle: Culture of access builds an able workforce
abstract: “RECRUITING DISABLED talent isn't an act of charity – it's what smart employers are doing to get ahead of the competition.” That is the view of the recently installed Minister for Disabled People, Health and Work, Justin Tomlinson. “There are 7.6 million working age people in the UK who have a disability, and many of them are more than able to work.”

articleTitle: The Teardown Samsung Galaxy note 10+ 5G: A mobile that's more about the battle for 5G-handset supremacy than practical use
abstract: SAMSUNG's latest fifth-generation mobile comms handset, the flagship Galaxy Note 10+ 5G, is, for all the engineering skill within it, something of an anomaly. If you are the kind of person comfortable with replacing your smartphone every 12 months and paying a premium price (starting at $1,300 — or £1,080 — for the 256GB model), there are aspects that recommend the device. But the overall message must be caveat emptor.

articleTitle: A step beyond fingerprints: DNA phenotyping and virtual autopsies — what are they and how are they and other new techniques, being used to unravel the secrets of crime scenes?
abstract: FORENSIC SCIENCE IS one of the most fascinating elements of the criminal justice system. It helps to prove cases ‘beyond reasonable doubt’ through the analysis of physical evidence. In everyday terms, it is the application of all the sciences to matters of law.

articleTitle: Gadgets
abstract: Get early adopter bragging rights with a developer model of this stunning folding smartphone. It's a 7.8-inch tablet with a flexible display, so you can fold it in half to transform it into a double-sided Android smartphone the size of a wallet.

articleTitle: H2O on the go!: Water could be the fuel source for running the emission-free engines of the future
abstract: IT SEEMS VEHICLES can run on most things these days: from batteries to hydrogen, to natural gas and even human waste. But how about water? This is what Australian-Israeli start-up Electriq∼Global claims can fuel vehicles from a bicycle to an articulated lorry, adding that it can outperform other fuels by twice the range at half the cost with no emissions.

articleTitle: Out, proud and at ease in the workplace
abstract: LGBTQ+ INCLUSION of employees in the workplace is still not a guarantee for every organisation. About one in five LGBT employees have experienced verbal bullying at work because of their sexual orientation, and people keep themselves ‘in the closet’ because they believe it would be career-limiting to be ‘out’.

articleTitle: Why it pays to be a male tech entrepreneur
abstract: JUST TWO PER CENT of venture capital (VC) money went to all-female founding teams in Europe in 2018, according to Atomico's State of European Tech report, while in the UK, for every £1 of VC investment, all-female founder teams get less than 1p, a British Business Bank report has revealed.

articleTitle: The teardown: Apple AirPod
abstract: THE FIRST COMMENT I want to make about Apple's second generation of AirPod wireless ear buds is that they are the first Apple product I have found it easy to convince my kids not to buy In fact, they convinced themselves.

articleTitle: Location location location: The emergency services have distributed a system which allows tracking the precise whereabouts of an individual to be achieved more efficiently… with the use of three simple words
abstract: IN THE EARLY part of last year, a young woman in the Humberside area of the UK was abducted and taken to a locked room where she had no idea of her location. But she could still dial the emergency services on her mobile phone. The operator was able to send her a text message containing a hyperlink, which enabled the phone to communicate with the worldwide Global Positioning System (GPS) to identify her location to within just a few feet and display it to her as a unique sequence of three words. The woman read that sequence out to the operator, who was then able to send a police car to the exact location.

articleTitle: The teardown macbook pro ‘butterfly’ keyboard: Apple has made yet further tweaks to its controversial laptop keyboard
abstract: LAST YEAR, APPLE acknowledged users were still having problems with the innovative ‘butterfly’ keys it introduced on higher-end laptops in 2015 — and put them through a third design rev as covered in our December 2018 Teardown.

articleTitle: Do you look like an engineer?
abstract: "SOMETIMES YOU DON'T want to go to the pub!" exclaims Dr Nike Folayan, a chartered engineer. However, when advancing in an engineering career still often involves informal bonding over beers, certain employees — most obviously Muslims — often struggle to feel they belong.

articleTitle: What is the material for a new age? We've had bronze age and iron age, arguably an oil and aluminium age. But what material will drive and define the world of tomorrow?
abstract: WHAT WILL BE the defining material of the next industrial age? In the past hundred years, steel gave way to oil and then silicon as information became the defining power behind industrial development. Will it return to energy, with hydrogen becoming a strong contender as a replacement for petroleum, or will renewables make lithium batteries central to future development? Or will other materials step in to propel industrial evolution further? Here are E&T's five contenders as the most likely candidate for the next materials age.

articleTitle: Imaging in a new dimension: Holographic and 3D visualisation companies are finding new ways to take the quality of holograms to the next level
abstract: The Idealised AI-designed woman who appears in an advertisement in ‘Blade Runner 2049’ shows how far the possibilities of holography continue to capture the imagination of science-fiction writers.

articleTitle: Book reviews: YouTubers, escape from earth, the women of the moon
abstract: YouTube, according to Chris Stokel-Walker, is a “kaleidoscope of visual and audio content that mimics the richness, quirkiness, beauty, and madness of human life”. In less than 15 years, the site has become the second most visited in the world. In the process, it has spawned its own communities, culture, celebrities, and a sector of employment which — if survey results are to be believed — is the most desired among school students today.

articleTitle: Magnetically charged particles at night… astronomers' delight!
abstract: IT'S A QUIET day at the Met Office Space Weather Operations Centre in Exeter. The centre takes up only one small corner in the giant hall occupied by dozens of weather forecasters working for the UK's national weather service. Large screens display complex weather models on every wall. In the space weather forecasting corner, two scientists are poring over a series of graphs and a range of satellite images capturing the solar disc in various colours. One small sunspot, a darker area on the surface of the Sun indicating reduced temperature due to changes to the magnetic field, is visible on the fiery sphere.

articleTitle: Lithium at any price? E&T confirms that major companies ‘mining’ brine for lithium in Chile's Atacama salt flats are reducing water levels in an already dry region, with detrimental consequences for local communities and the environment
abstract: GLOBAL LITHIUM DEMAND is soaring, as climate pressures drive a switch to electric vehicles that use the metal in their batteries. Therein lies a conflict: supply needs to increase for environmental reasons but lithium mining harms the environment.

articleTitle: DIY science down on the farm: A group of retired British engineers have set themselves the task of building an environmentally friendly reactor that can circumvent conventional shortcomings in hydrogen production while producing aluminium oxide and heat. E&T went to see the project
abstract: AT THE GATES of a farm featuring a ‘Keep Out’ sign, E&T is greeted by a smiling cockney man wearing a T-shirt with five colourful test tubes printed on it. Alan Smith, 74, together with a team of other pensioners, runs a self-built hydrogen reactor in a former milking parlour in rural Essex.

articleTitle: The no drone zone
abstract: ON WEDNESDAY 19 December 2018, London's Gatwick Airport received a startling wake-up call: drone sightings were reported in the restricted airspace. The airport was forced to suspend operations just as thousands of travellers were heading there to get home or get away for Christmas.

articleTitle: Quantum radars: Expose stealth planes
abstract: RADAR TECHNOLOGY HAS become an ever more important tool in warfare since the Second World War, used to monitor the electromagnetic spectrum to detect and track enemy aircraft, missiles, satellites and other systems that in turn have grown more sophisticated in evading detection.

articleTitle: Quantum on the Money
abstract: OPINION IS DIVIDED over when quantum computers will enter the commercial mainstream: IBM reckons four to five years; more conservative forecasts suggest not for a decade, at least. Whichever timeframe proves correct, it's probable that the financial services sector will be foremost to adopt quantum tech for line-of-business applications — and to bear the brunt of the challenges that early adopters always face.

articleTitle: The whole story of… parking: The world of parking is no longer stationary
abstract: While some of us take enormous pride in swiftly reversing a car back into a tight spot, most people find the act of finding a space and parking a car tedious — if not stressful. Why not let a robot do it for you?

articleTitle: The teardown: Apple iPad pro
abstract: “WHILE WE ANTICIPATED some challenges in key emerging markets, we did not foresee the magnitude of the economic deceleration, particularly in Greater China. In fact, most of our revenue shortfall to our guidance, and over 100 per cent of our year-over-year worldwide revenue decline, occurred in Greater China across iPhone, Mac and iPad.” Tim Cook, CEO, Apple, 2 January 2019, Q4 Letter to Investors.

articleTitle: GCHQ: A century of ciphers
abstract: IN 1919, with the end of the First World War still ringing in the nation's memory, Britain was already putting in place intelligence countermeasures to ensure it would maintain the upper hand, should such conflicts ever happen again. By the time the Armistice was signed on 11 November 1918, four years and three months of industrialised slaughter had left just over 700,000 British soldiers dead. Within a year, on the recommendation of Lord Curzon, the British Army and Royal Navy intelligence services — M11b and ‘Room 40’ — were merged to form the Government Code and Cypher School (GC&CS). Located at Watergate House, London, the GC&CS was in the century that followed to become the Government Communications Headquarters, commonly known as GCHQ, arguably the most famous national government intelligence agency in the world.

articleTitle: OEMs gear up for mobility as a service
abstract: MOBILITY-AS-A-SERVICE is coming to the car sector, which means digitally enabled car-sharing and ride-hailing is set to overtake the traditional model of manufacture and sale of cars — and manufacturers need to be ready.

articleTitle: The tear down: Samsung Galaxy Watch
abstract: CELLPHONES KILLED wristwatches. Smartphone makers have been trying to resurrect them. This ironic contrast has dogged the efforts of companies like Samsung and Apple. But with the launch of the Samsung Galaxy Watch, might we now say it has been resolved?

articleTitle: Millbrook takes the virtual track
abstract: YOU CAN'T PUT a price on anyone's life, so it is quite understandable that we expect car manufacturers to treat safety as a basic requirement — not a ‘nice to have’. The testing required to get to this level is already considerable, but the arrival of autonomous cars will see test demands increase dramatically.

articleTitle: Pollutant or resource?: Six ideas for CO2 reuse
abstract: THE WORLD WILL have to start removing 12 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide from the Earth's atmosphere every year by 2050 if it wants to limit global warming to the relatively safe 1.5°C compared to pre-industrial times, according to the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change.

articleTitle: Aking stock in uncertainty
abstract: AS THIS MAGAZINE goes to print, it is still largely unclear exactly what will happen on 29 March. Will Britain leave the European Union as scheduled? And, if so, will it face either a transition period or leap over the ‘No Deal’ precipice?

articleTitle: The problem with plastic
abstract: LAST YEAR, 2.26 million tonnes of plastic packaging was ‘placed on the market’, according to The UK Household Plastics Collection Survey 2018 commissioned by RECycling of Used Plastics Limited (RECOUP). Around half of that(1.12 tonnes) was used by households and almost half of that (537,000 tonnes) was collected for recycling. Sixty-six per cent was exported, while the rest was recycled in the UK.

articleTitle: Industry benefits from the digital baby boom
abstract: WHILE IT SO OFTEN struggles to move on from its tried and tested past, the manufacturing industry is nonetheless a driving force when it comes to the application of new technology. This digital age — the fourth industrial revolution — when looked at historically will seem like the blink of an eye, but such are the radical changes in technology involved that not everyone is immediately reaching for the digital switch.

articleTitle: Out with the old, in with the twin
abstract: IN THE CASE OF the architectural and construction sector, the digital twin arrives as an upgrade on its worthy predecessor, BIM. Building information modelling has been around for over a decade and theoretically stays with a building through its concept, design, construction and operation. The problem with BIM, according to Howard Tee, CTO of Newtecnic, is that it is misused both as a term and in its function.

articleTitle: Plundering the deep blue sea
abstract: THE TECHNOLOGICAL developments required to exploit the resources known to exist in the harsh deep-sea environment are, although considerable, perhaps the least of the industry's worries. After all, it can draw on the experiences of the offshore energy industry, where operations at depths of 3–4km are now almost routine.

articleTitle: Six common packaging and recycling myths
abstract: Manufacturers of biodegradable and compostable packaging claim it is more sustainable and environmentally friendly than plastics because it is made from a renewable carbon source — plant-based materials, such as corn oil, starch, and plants — and because it will eventually break down in the environment.

articleTitle: British rocketeers in the new space age
abstract: WHEN THE UK government announced plans to have rocket launches conducted from British soil as early as 2020, many questioned the feasibility of such a vision especially the ambitious timeline.

articleTitle: First ‘soundless’ aeroplane takes flight
abstract: IMAGINE AN AIRCRAFT that is almost completely silent, powered by an engine with no moving parts. Such apparent science fiction became a reality when, last November, scientists from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) flew the first ever ‘ion drive’ aeroplane.

articleTitle: Hybrids on the high
abstract: THE DREAM IS ALLURING. A sleek ship on a sparkling sea, set against a sky of the purest blue, cleanliness and healthiness embodied in luxury. The reality is painfully different. Shipping is a major contributor to pollution and greenhouse gas emissions, responsible for an estimated 15 per cent of nitrogen oxide (NOx) and 8 per cent of sulfur gas emissions, said the Independent in February 2018. According to figures originally published in the Guardian in 2009, one giant container ship can emit almost the same amount of cancer- and asthma-causing chemicals as 50 million cars, and around 50,000 premature deaths in Europe have been attributed to international shipping.

articleTitle: Are wildfires getting worse
abstract: 2018 WAS A bad year for wildfires. Regions as diverse as the Mediterranean and the Arctic Circle were exceptionally hard hit, and the wildfires in California caught the world's headlines. Even moorlands near Manchester were ravaged by flames and declared a major incident. Frightened residents who were evacuated from nearby villages described the fire as an “apocalypse” and a “towering inferno”, and thick plumes of smoke were visible from space.

articleTitle: Scared sili
abstract: SILICONES, like plastics, were invented in the 20th century and have since become a colourful, omnipresent part of our lives. Silicones are made of repeating units of siloxanes: silicon-oxygen chains. In their many forms — oils, gels, foams and solids — they are valuable in electronics, medicine, transport and other industries; significantly, their unique sets of properties help improve energy efficiency and reduce waste (they tend to be very light and durable, and make excellent thermal insulators and lubricants).

articleTitle: Dark side of the vinyl: Are records bad for the environment?
abstract: VINYL RECORDS are back. The irrepressible format that many people thought had died off in the mid-noughties has come roaring back over the past decade, hitting sales heights not seen since 1991, the last high-water mark for vinyl record sales.

articleTitle: Life in the old box
abstract: I AM RUNNING late for an interview in central London and would normally be stressed about the time required to negotiate some endless office corridors before I can face my interviewee. In this case, however, I have no such worries, because the address in my notebook is laconic: Sicilian Avenue, Holborn, Red Phone Box.

articleTitle: A new dimension to surgery
abstract: WHEN DELIVERING BAD news, you may not expect a neurosurgeon to ask you to wear a headset and grab a gaming controller — but doing so is proving an effective part of pre-surgical consultations. Virtual reality (VR) is easing anxiety for patients facing neurosurgery.

articleTitle: The tear down: Zanco tiny t1 handset
abstract: NOT ALL CROWDFUNDING projects succeed. Kickstarter says that just 37 per cent of those that have used its platform have been ‘successful’. But among the failures, those where a product is prototyped, made in volume and then sold are rare. The Zanco tiny t1 is such an outlier. It is also, to date, the world's smallest mobile phone.

articleTitle: Quantum transform travel
abstract: AS CARS BECOME increasingly connected and aircraft ever more sensor-laden, automotive and aerospace companies are making a transition from being ‘nuts and bolts’ manufacturers to so-called ‘mobility companies’ that collect and use unprecedented amounts of data.

articleTitle: How to save the world in 12 years
abstract: VAGUE PROMISES ARE no longer enough. Action and commitment are needed, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) stated in their 2018 ‘Special Report on Global Warming of 1.5°C’. If the world fails to rise to the challenge, global temperatures will likely soar past the relatively safe 1.5°C threshold. The consequences could be severe — extreme heat waves and droughts, mass extinction and a dangerous sea-level rise.

articleTitle: Are role models the answer?
abstract: ONE HUNDRED YEARS ago this year, a small committee of influential women — designers, munitions factory managers and wives of eminent engineers — gathered together to found the Women's Engineering Society (WES). It was a time of hope. The First World War had ended and limited women's suffrage had been won. In the Society's first Woman Engineer Journal, the declared aim was to "encourage and stimulate all women who are interested in engineering" and "be a means towards removing the prejudices and artificial restrictions which now prevent women from taking up engineering as a trade or profession". (The Journal is now fully digitalised, indexed and freely available.) The women who'd gathered together on 23 June 1919 sensed a new dawn.

articleTitle: Be still, my beeping heart
abstract: WE HAVE BEEN recreating human anatomy for tens of thousands of years: from Palaeolithic carvings of exaggeratedly fertile women to the disturbingly sensual Anatomical Venus' sculpted from wax in the 18th century. Today, scientists are building increasingly complex models of the human body, moving from wax and marble to working in the digital realm.

articleTitle: Legislation new laws: Is technology running away from the law?
abstract: THE LEGAL SYSTEM has always had trouble keeping pace with technology. The introduction of motor vehicles, first in the form of steam engines and then with the petrol engine, shows how politicians can veer from one extreme to another as the market develops. First subject to stringent controls, the trend moved to liberalisation that then led to horrifying accidents and a subsequent tightening. In a world where artificial intelligence, space exploration and biotechnology are all moving quickly, it seems obvious that governments should look hard at what current laws allow and what loopholes have emerged. And though some of the possible new laws seem obvious, there is ready potential for mistakes.

articleTitle: Does Brexit pull the plug on the UK energy sector?
abstract: THE UNITED KINGDOM'S power grid is fully integrated with mainland Europe's, so given the evidently Herculean task of severing ties with the European Union, it is unsurprising that concerns have been raised about post-Brexit energy policy.

articleTitle: Siblings make sense of smart cities
abstract: WOULD THE PERFECT CITY have open spaces and plenty of natural light? Would travel between any two parts be simple and fast? Would development be structured and sympathetic to the rest of the city? These issues and many more could be resolved by generating a digital replica — a virtual city that becomes the basis for all future change and growth.

articleTitle: Why the world needs wetlands
abstract: THE UK'S BIGGEST wetlands restoration project was completed last year It took almost a decade, and now thousands of sea birds and waders congregate on Wallasea Island — avocet, black-headed gulls, golden plovers, teal, redshank and lapwing, and soon, hopefully, rare spoonbills, black-winged stilts and Kentish plover.

articleTitle: Plastics on point
abstract: THERE ARE MANY situations where plastics remain the best option because of the properties they can provide — it's a testament to the extraordinary properties of carbon, though its Group IV neighbour from the periodic table, silicon, has also proved to be a strong contender. Improved technology, as discussed elsewhere in this issue, may improve susta inability in the future. But for the here and now, here are six reasons why carbon and silicon polymers remain so prevalent.

articleTitle: An inside view
abstract: FOR THOSE of you who haven't already tried it out, augmented reality (AR) superimposes digital information in text or graphics onto a live view of the real world. For the most immersive experience you can try it through one of the new wearable devices like Microsoft HoloLens or Oculus Rift, but it also works just fine with a smartphone running an AR app, as we show you in my screenshots here.

articleTitle: Is the future meatless?
abstract: AS OUR POPULATION soars, there is more pressure to keep us fed. By 2050, the global population is estimated to reach 9.6 billion. According to World Resources Institute, food production needs to rise by 61 per cent by then to keep up with demand.

articleTitle: Have your packaging and eat it
abstract: NEARLY 10 YEARS AGO, Professor Nory Mulyono started making packaging from seaweed in a room in her fiancé's house. Heavy rains in her home city of Jakarta had yet again highlighted the painful problem of plastic, with piles of waste swept away from municipal landfills and washed up on shorelines.

articleTitle: Plastics with potential
abstract: IN 2016, a 17-strong team of executives and analysts working for the Ellen MacArthur Foundation claimed that by 2050 the world's oceans are expected to contain, by weight, more plastics than fish. For three years they had pored over hundreds of pieces of literature while consulting more than 180 researchers, engineers and policy-makers from universities, industry and government.

articleTitle: Beyond bricks and mortar 5 innovative materials
abstract: WHAT'S THE MOST widely used manmade material in the world? It surrounds you day and night — when you work, when you're entertained and when you sleep.

articleTitle: China's tsunami of waste
abstract: ANYONE SEEKING TO understand the enormity of the plastic waste problem faced by China should watch the award-winning documentary ‘Plastic China’.

articleTitle: Data DNA and diamonds
abstract: WE LIVE IN a data age. So much so that the numbers describing our data consumption are now too large to grasp. For example, 2.5 quintillion bytes of data are created every day (that's a one with 18 zeroes after it). This rate is only increasing, with 90 per cent of all the data that currently exists being generated in just the last two years.

articleTitle: Why biodegradable don't solve the plastic pollution problem
abstract: "POLYETHYLENE terephthalate, or PET, which plastic water bottles are made of, is a remarkable polymer," says Professor Alex Conradie, who leads the Sustainable Process Technologies research group at the University of Nottingham. "It has very useful properties and given decades of process optimisation invested into PET manufacturing, it's also very cost effective. It is a tall order to match the properties of such a versatile material."

articleTitle: The teardown: Apple Mac mini
abstract: IT HAS BEEN a little more than four years since Apple last visited its Mac mini desktop computer. The new version is more ‘professional grade’ than its predecessors. That is reflected in a sizeable price hike from £499 to £799. You can go a lot higher too, if you add many of its options.

articleTitle: Is China returning to coal-fired power?
abstract: CHINA MIGHT BE U-turning back towards dirty coal-fired power Results of a new study found that the country has restarted construction on more than 50GW of suspended coal-fired power plants: as much as the entire coal fleet of Africa and the Middle East.

articleTitle: Unleashing quantum into the world
abstract: SINCE JUNE 2018, Cambridge University researchers and their co-workers at Toshiba Research Europe at the Cambridge Science Park have a new way of communicating. They use quantum states of photons to exchange secret keys to encrypted messages via a conventional optical fibre. The set-up, the UK's first city-scale quantum network, is intended to prove that quantum key distribution (QKD), a technique enabling what is believed to be an unhackable exchange of secret information, is ready to enter the commercial market.

articleTitle: Cyber security shipping: Cyber pirates terrorise the high seas
abstract: TODAY'S PIRATES are just as innovative in the tactics and technologies they use as they were in historic times. Where once the likes of Henry Morgan, Captain Kidd and Blackbeard boarded ships and stole cargo, the modern-day pirate relies not on a cutlass but on hacking skills to obtain more ill-gotten gains than Blackbeard could ever have dreamed of.

articleTitle: Editor's letter
abstract: AT THIS TIME of year, for several years now, we have been running a women in engineering special issue. We get mixed reactions. Most responses are supportive but we also hear the question: "What's all this got to do with engineering?"

articleTitle: Bizarre tech
abstract: It's almost the end of the year, so you may think I've run out of things to lightly mock. But you are so very wrong. This month, here's two potential Christmas gifts and something to wrap them with. Enjoy!

articleTitle: Your letter
abstract: In a recent ‘View from Brussels’ column for the E&T website, Sam Morgan reports on how electricscooter-sharing schemes that have sprung up in many of Europe's capital cities are proving to be hugely popular, but that problems and public pushback have already started to emerge.

articleTitle: Your letters
abstract: With reference to the debate about whether or not to use equipment from the Chinese manufacturer Huawei in the UK's proposed 5G network upgrade, it is sobering to recall that in the 1980s and 1990s the entire national telephone network was upgraded from analogue to digital using equipment which was largely designed and manufactured in this country.

articleTitle: Editor's letter
abstract: 2020 HAS LONG been a landmark year. Not for any particularly good reason other than it provided a nice round number, which, like 2000, once seemed a long, long way off.

articleTitle: Dear evil engineer: Could I build a freeze ray that's appropriate to my icy new persona?
abstract: Hail Evil Engineer, I have recently undergone a chilling experience, which has left me a different man. I hope you may be able to help me adjust to my new life.

articleTitle: Dear evil engineer: Could I use sharks with laser beams to entertain my guests?
abstract: Dear Evil Engineer, I hope you may be able to provide an engineering solution to an embarrassing problem I've been faced with.

articleTitle: Your letters: Engtechletters@theiet.org
abstract: Send your letters to The Editor, E&T, Michael Faraday House, Six Hills Way, Stevenage, Herts SG1 2AY, UK, or to engtechletters@theiet.org. We reserve the right to edit letters and to use submissions in any other format.

articleTitle: Editor's letter
abstract: IN THIS ISSUE we take you to beyond the end of the world: from the various impending dooms, through the most likely — or rather least unlikely — cataclysms, how to avoid them, survive them and finally how to rebuild.

articleTitle: Dear evil engineer: Modern prosthetics may bring a whole new meaning to firearms
abstract: Dear Evil Engineer, I breed and train crocodiles, which I sell to villains in want of exotic pets. My most senior henchman recently got into an altercation with my prized crocodilian stud, and he unfortunately lost his lower left arm to the beast.

articleTitle: Buzz words
abstract: Picture this. You're seamlessly scrolling through Zoopla or RightMove and you find the house of your dreams. You're ever so persistent in putting an offer on the house, but you have yet to find out whether you can get a mortgage to help invest in the property. It is very often that people lose out on their ideal home due to the long mortgagelending processes put in place.

articleTitle: Your letters
abstract: The recent blackout incident on the UK power grid means that the subject of grid-frequency regulation and inertia has received widespread coverage. The reduction in conventional power generation using rotating machines and boilers with their inherent stored energy reserves has resulted in a more rapid response of system frequency to a loss of generation. In principle, it is possible for renewable sources such as wind and solar PV to replicate the inertia and droop characteristics of rotating steam plant, but only by operating continuously at below the maximum available output, resulting in added cost and loss of precious low-carbon power, or by adding an energy store.

articleTitle: Comment: Additive manufacturing can give past treasures a new lease of life
abstract: GEORGE SANTAYANA once said that "those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it." History, as Santayana would see it, allows us to understand why we live the way we do — and why it varies across the globe. Displays of historical treasures from different periods of time provide us with an even deeper understanding.

articleTitle: Dear evil engineer: Could I spite my old rival by shooting down his satellite?
abstract: Dear Evil Engineer, I have had a long-running rivalry with a villain (who shall remain unnamed). We have plotted against each other since we attended university together, and he took credit for my scheme to hide durian fruit in the university library during the sweltering summer exam season. Since then he has always worked to undermine me, including bribing some of my most-valued staff to defect to his operations.

articleTitle: Editor's letter
abstract: THIS MONTH'S cover features our modelling-clay hero from the Pliocene — Dug from the Aardman Animation production ‘Early Man’. His Stone Age, the first great age, lasted millions of years. In contrast, the Plastics Age is only around a century old and environmentalists are already hoping it's the beginning of its end. The more recent Silicon Age is barely half a century old.

articleTitle: Your letters engtechletters@theiet.org: Send your letters to The Editor, E&T, Michael Faraday House, Six Hills Way, Stevenage, Herts SG1 2AY, UK, or to engtechletters@theiet.org. We reserve the right to edit letters and to use submissions in any other format
abstract: I was interested to read the story in the July 2019 issue of E&T about the University of British Columbia's work on smart-meter security. The major issue with smart meters fitted with a supply-control switch is the ability to switch off the power to the house. An attack that achieves this on a large scale and disables meters such that they cannot be switched back on again is probably the most severe risk, as every home affected would require a visit to restore the meter. With more than 13 million SMETS1 meters installed in the UK, a successful attack on even 1 per cent would be severe.

articleTitle: Comment: The past decade has seen many companies piloting so-called ‘Industry 4.0’ technologies, but how can this new set of tools take hold when there's no real sense of what they can do for manufacturing as a whole?
abstract: IT's NEARLY TEN YEARS since Industry 4.0 was first hailed as the next big transformation in manufacturing. “I4.0! The Fourth Industrial Revolution!” It was going to be all-consuming, covering robotics, advanced manufacturing processes such as 3D printing and the digitisation of the factory and the supply chain.

articleTitle: Dear evil engineer: How can I earn renown by killing all of those pesky bumblebees?
abstract: Dear Evil Engineer My villainous schemes have always been modest; I am an expert in making children cry, home invasions, and mobbing family picnics with my gang. Since entering middle age, I have set my sights on more ambitious schemes. I hate everything about bumblebees — from their cute fuzzy hides to their good PR — and I am no longer content with merely raiding their hives and feeding them to our spawn. How could I kill them all?

articleTitle: Comment: Graphene innovations will make future homes smart from the start
abstract: THE MASSIVE surge in interest in smart-home technology over the last decade has made voice-controlled devices the latest must-have consumer gadget. Amazon alone has sold over a million Alexa-enabled devices, manufactured by 4,500 different companies, and the Amazon store stocks more than 3,000 Google Assistant devices, 580 Cortana devices and 390 that use Siri.

articleTitle: BuzzWords: From the consequences of Brexit to military information in a pair of glasses, here's what makes words such as ‘robotics’ and ‘augmented reality’ stick in our brains
abstract: The Brexit deadline is just around the corner, and it's clear that not everyone is going to be best pleased with the outcome, whatever it is. In fact, the mere idea of leaving the European Union still sits uncomfortably with many. Among them are researchers in the healthcare sector, particularly in robotics surgery, who are anxious about the UK's likely departure… and according to a new analysis, led by Imperial College London, collaborations with EU researchers and institutions have been critical to the UK's success in robotic surgery research and innovation.

articleTitle: After all: Our columnist reveals his favourite French town and its unique engineering heritage
abstract: NOTHING ABOUT Montreuilsur-Mer is what you expect. To begin with, it's not quite ‘sur mer’, but is built on a silted-up river estuary, about 20 miles away from the actual sea. First-time visitors tend to be swept off their feet by the unexpected charm and beauty of that seemingly unremarkable small town in the north of France, a mere 45-minute drive from the Port of Calais. It happened to me about 20 years ago when I first stepped on the town's ancient cobbles, still remembering the touch of the wheels of the cart in Victor Hugo's ‘Les Miserables’ that ran down the old man Fauchelevent, only for him to be saved when reformed convict Jean Valjean famously lifted up the cart with his bare hands.

articleTitle: Bizarre tech: In this month's supercharged column: A device that turns you into a ‘superhero’ by sticking a light in your earhole, a knee brace that makes you a phone charger, and a poop-storing box
abstract: Brace yourselves for unlimited power! This lightweight knee brace, as described in Applied Physics Letters, could extract energy from a person's movement to charge medical devices, wearables, or even a phone. What would make this knee brace extra cool was if it was to, you know, brace a knee.

articleTitle: View from Washington: Will the high-profile collapse of we's initial public offering (IPO) force a rethink about letting get-big-fast unicorns dominate investment and innovation?
abstract: GET BIG FAST (GBF), be a unicorn and change the world. It feels like we have been living with the GBF formula in innovation and investment for more than a decade, but is change on the way? Is the big signal September's spectacular collapse of an IPO (initial public offering) by The We Company, parent of the WeWork shared-workspace venture?

articleTitle: Editor's letter: ‘To infinity, and beyond’… far, far beyond, as we find out in our summer special on exploration
abstract: “I WANT to be an explorer, like Magellan,” Truman declares to the class in one of my favourite scenes from the 1998 film starring Jim Carrey. “I'm afraid no one's going to pay you to do that, Truman,” says his teacher. “You might have to find something a little more practical. Besides, you're too late. There's really nothing left to explore.”

articleTitle: The eccentric engineer: Bringing sound to the silver screen with a cartoon mouse
abstract: THE HISTORY OF sound engineering is intimately tied up with the history of the movies and the desire to make the experience of a film as real as possible, so it's perhaps not surprising that modern recorded music owes a great debt to a certain fictional mouse.

articleTitle: Comment: More directors and managers are being prosecuted for health and safety offences. Why is this happening, and will it lead to safer workplaces?
abstract: IN APRIL this year, the Sentencing Council, which produces advice on sentencing for courts in England and Wales, published an impact assessment of new guidelines for health and safety offences that took effect in February 2016. It reported that since 2011 the number of individuals prosecuted for health and safety offences has steadily increased and that in 2017 more than a quarter of those convicted received an immediate or suspended prison sentence.

articleTitle: View from Brussels: An EU plan to scrap the bi-annual change of clocks has stalled, after it initially seemed as if 2019 would be the last year of ‘spring forward, fall back’
abstract: IN 2018, THE European Commission asked millions of Europeans whether they were fed up with changing their clocks twice a year. The overwhelming majority said they would prefer to stick to the same time-zone all the time.

articleTitle: Money markets: Richard Branson's Virgin Galactic has floated on the New York Stock Exchange, and the exciting potential for investing in space companies looks almost infinite
abstract: IN THE stock market there are a lot of investment sayings that are right a little bit more than half of the time. One is ‘Up like a rocket and down like a rock’.

articleTitle: After all: From ‘alienation zone’ to the ‘secret’ engineering dream town
abstract: WHAT IS IT about the English Channel that makes its crossing a matter of prime significance for so many? For decades, people have been travelling across it on all kinds of vessels — from state-of-the art ferry boats to surfboards and bathtubs. During the last hundred or so years, they have also flown across the Channel in all sorts of flying machines, propelled by steam, petrol, solar energy, or just pedals. The latest person to take up the challenge was French inventor Franky Zapata, who — after a couple of failed attempts — carried out a 35km-long cross-Channel hop in August on a bespoke jet-powered hoverboard (see bit.ly/channel0919).

articleTitle: Comment: Time for industry to burst the bubble on buzzwords
abstract: I'M RAPIDLY APPROACHING the end of my third decade in the enterprise B2B technology sector, an industry that has become a grand master in spin. It has gorged on the creation and promotion of acronyms, buzzwords and hyperbole that power the industry's marketing machine. In many cases it's an attempt to differentiate between mediocre technology in an overly crowded market or to position a solution as solving a business problem that no one knew existed.

articleTitle: Bizarre tech: This month, I've found some special bits and pieces for you to enjoy: A wearable for dinosaur fans, a life-saving craft, and a blood test that tells you when you'll die. Nice!
abstract: Every dinosaur enthusiast's fantasy Na na naaaa na na, na na naaaa na na, na na naaaa, na naaaa, na naaaaaa. If you don't know what that is, it's my written version of the ‘Jurassic Park’ opening theme song. Read it back. There you go.

articleTitle: Your letters: Credit the engineers who delivered Apollo 11 pictures
abstract: As a radio engineer I was sad to note that in all the celebrations of the 50th anniversary of the Apollo 11 Moon landing, the role of radio communication has been largely ignored. Millions watched Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin taking their first steps on the Moon's surface, but there were no plaudits for the engineers who made the transmission of those images possible.

articleTitle: Editor's letter
abstract: HE'S MOST FAMOUS as a painter but should be equally remembered for his science and engineering — and much more besides. Leonardo da Vinci was a prolific inventor and ideas man for everything from ball bearings to bridges (p18). The original Renaissance Man. He even thought through the problems of city planning, sketching out his own version of the New Town 500 years ago (p40). Some of his designs were instant hits and are still with us today, like the canal lock. Others seemed fantastical but turned out to be just hundreds of years ahead of their time.

articleTitle: The eccentric engineer: How a gardener, a small girl and a giant-leafed Amazon lily built a crystal palace fit for English aristocrats
abstract: AS ANY GOOD engineer can tell you, art often imitates nature — it is always a good first place to look when on the hunt for new engineering ideas. Never was this truer than in the case of a gardener, a small girl and a giant leaf.

articleTitle: Dear evil engineer: Could I replace my machine guns with steam cannons?
abstract: Dear Evil Engineer, I write this correspondence with a quill on vellum, sitting in my castle full of chain-bedecked skeletons and historic torture devices. I enjoy antiquity. It weighs heavy on my heart that in order to keep pace with my villainous peers, I have had to install a computer and router in my dungeon, acquire a horseless carriage to ride to appointments, and replace my henchmen's plate armour and longswords with bullet-proof garments and machine guns. While this is inconsistent with my brand, I will reluctantly do what is necessary to remain competitive in the sector.

articleTitle: View from brussels: Climate change policy has gone mainstream in Brussels, but now attention has shifted to finance. A decision on funding fossil fuels could be monumental
abstract: AS GREEN PROTESTS reach new heights of participation and media coverage, EU countries stand on the brink of agreeing a pact that will see the bloc go carbon-neutral by 2050.

articleTitle: Your letters
abstract: I was sad to see the December 2018/January 2019 issue of E&T magazine, if not glorifying war, then at least treating it as if it were a morally neutral part of life. It is not. War wrecks lives, wreaks environmental havoc, damages whole generations, creates refugees and generates migrant crises. It is an extravagant waste of resources and a blight on all those who wish to lead a settled, decent life. And, of course, it sows the seeds of terrorism. As for the cover — ‘take the soldier out of war’ — do we really want to build a world where those who suffer most from wars are everyone except the soldiers?

articleTitle: Comment: It's time the tech sector took responsibility for its talent pipelines
abstract: RESEARCH PUBLISHED last year on behalf of the educational charity EDT has shown just how dominant technology jobs are in the UK STEM jobs market. Of the skills required for the most common STEM job postings in 2017, 87 per cent were IT related, and more than half of these were for programming and software-development skills. This is creating high and continuing pressure on a limited tech talent pool in the UK.

articleTitle: Your letters
abstract: Social media has been in the public eye a lot lately, spurred on by 14-year-old Molly Russell's suicide and many other incidents of ‘bullying anonymously from a distance’. My own daughter, aged 15, was subjected to abuse from two ‘friends’ on Instagram a few years ago. Even now she receives counselling for anxiety attacks, which she attributes to that unpleasant period in her life.
