articleTitle: Comment: Profession's breadth must not be a barrier to influencing policy
abstract: ENGINEERING PROVIDES the backbone of the UK's industry and economy, and greatly benefits people's everyday lives. The sector generates 23 per cent of the country's total turnover and accounts for nearly half its exports. Engineers have insights and skills that can help address significant challenges like improving productivity, harnessing disruptive technological change for public good, and upgrading infrastructure, energy and transport systems.

articleTitle: Dear evil engineer: How can I cryogenically freeze my enemies to keep for future taunting?
abstract: Dear Evil Engineer, I'm sure you are familiar with the debate within the villainy community about the benefits and drawbacks of keeping captured enemies alive for the purposes of boasting and taunting. I have always believed that a quick death by gunshot is too good for my enemies, and follow a policy of keeping them alive until I tire of them.

articleTitle: Evil engineer: How could I steal the Moon and become a star?
abstract: Dear Evil Engineer, I have enjoyed a successful career, and was recently included in a list of Villainous Disruptors of 2018 published by Evil & Treachery (E&T). Other villains reaching this stage in their careers may be ready to hang up the Mao suit and settle into quiet retirement. However, I still have all the plucky ambition of a pre-2018 Elon Musk, combined with four decades of experience managing high-impact evil operations with a global reach.

abstract: Dear Evil Engineer, Last week, it was my turn to host the International Association for Synergistic eVillainy's monthly board meeting. I had recently been appointed ordinary committee member, and was glad to play host to such esteemed company.

articleTitle: Your letters
abstract: I was disappointed to read Chris Hayward's letter in the February 2019 issue of E&T, likening members of our profession who work in the defence industry to slave traders and torturers. Engineers put technology into society's hands; it's not always possible to predict whether society will use it to do good or bad.

articleTitle: Comment: Make your business more agile — one step at a time
abstract: AGILE WORKING WAS born out of software development. It was developed and refined by tech teams as a way of working that sped delivery to market. But now it's been adopted much more widely, with great success. Recent research carried out by PA Consulting on organisational agility found the top 10 per cent of businesses by financial performance are almost 30 per cent more likely to display agile characteristics.

articleTitle: Comment: Market failures could see Britain suffering five-day power cuts
abstract: EVEN IN INDUSTRIALISED nations in the 21st century, the sort of electricity-grid system failure that's been seen in parts of Australia in recent years is not uncommon. And in the UK, the risk of total blackout or significant partial shutdown of the transmission network is increasing.

articleTitle: Dear evil engineer: Can I hack Trident and destroy Belgium from my bedroom?
abstract: Dear Evil Engineer, I have been reading about the exciting opportunities to take advantage of security failings in Evil & Treachery (E&T) Magazine. I am astonished time and time again by the ignorance and incompetence of government officials when it comes to cyber security.

articleTitle: Editor's letters
abstract: HOW FAR IS a quantum leap? In science it's the sudden change in an electron's energy-level known as atomic electron transition. In everyday speech it's come to mean an extreme change leading to a whole new level. That's how quantum computing will appear after conventional computing.

articleTitle: Off-the-grid thinking to end Nigeria's blackouts
abstract: FIVE YEARS after the privatisation of Nigeria's power sector, even the most luxurious Lagos hotels still suffer daily blackouts. The size of the gap between the country's energy needs and its current provision is daunting.

articleTitle: Your letters
abstract: The UK government's discussion of the possibility of stopping new housing developments from having domestic gas feeds brings up several points. Is gas less efficient in terms of heating and cooking than electricity, by direct comparison of kilowatt-hours? It is easy to imagine that much heat escapes from gas boilers and cookers compared with electric alternatives. There are also higher pollution levels locally, without the cleaning advantage of large-scale furnaces. Converting fossil fuel to electricity at the point of import or extraction would save a fortune in doing away with most of the gas network and avoid maintaining two energy-distribution networks.

abstract: BRONTE LOOKS like death. Has something terrible happened? "Is the band still going?" I ask. "Yeah, we've got three gigs in Liverpool this week."

abstract: A PARCEL ARRIVES with our business cards inside. We unpack the boxes and discover we are all ‘researchers’.

articleTitle: Editor's letters
abstract: PLASTIC WAS THE material that shaped the 20th century Invented well over 100 years ago, plastics really took off mid-century as the range grew, engineers found more applications, and designers learnt how to use the material to its best advantage. As the young Ben (played by Dustin Hoffman) was advised in the 1967 film ‘The Graduate’, "there's a great future in plastics". At the risk of sounding like a boring uncle, it may not have been very appealing to young people of the time like Ben, but it was actually sound career advice. Manufacturers have now made a tonne of plastics for every person alive in the world today Plastics are everywhere — and unfortunately just about everywhere they shouldn't be.

articleTitle: System boosts smart meter resilience to cyber attacks
abstract: A TEAM AT the University of British Columbia in Canada has been working on a system to greatly improve the resilience of smart meters to hacking.

articleTitle: Photo essay: Norfolk's sandscaping project
abstract: FIVE YEARS in the planning, the 6km-long dune will protect Bacton Terminal — which supplies one-third of the UK's gas — from erosion that has left parts of the site just metres from a cliff edge.

abstract: RESEARCHERS at the University of Exeter have found that robotic pets could benefit older people living in care homes, providing much of the pleasure and comfort of real pets, as well as increasing social activity.

abstract: UNIFIED DIGITAL MAPS of underground pipes and cables are being created in north-east England and London in pilot projects that are intended to pave the way for a national register of underground assets.

abstract: Harley-Davidson revealed LiveWire, its first ever electric production motorcycle, at CES 2019 in Las Vegas last month.

articleTitle: The eccentric engineer: This edition tells the story of how Isambard Kingdom Brunel, voted second greatest Briton of all time, floated into the unreliable clutches of the first iron-built ship
abstract: ENGINEERS DON'T always get the credit they deserve, but if there's one who does, it's Isambard Kingdom Brunel, voted second greatest Briton of all time in a BBC poll in 2002 (after Churchill). However, as with all celebrities, he also tends to get a lot of the credit others deserve, and some perhaps that no-one does.

articleTitle: Interview Maggie Aderin-Pocock: Words and portrait
abstract: "MY APPROACH TO science is to make it entertaining," says Maggie Aderin-Pocock, tireless champion for the public understanding of science. At one end of the spectrum, she promotes applied technology on mass broadcast television; at the other she's passionate about grass roots communication in schools. An engineer with decades of experience in designing instrumentation for space and terrestrial telescopes, she's well-known in academia, industry and the media.

articleTitle: Human rights: Political opposition growing to police technology in the UK
abstract: MPS AND human-rights technology groups have called for UK police forces to cease all use of facial-recognition surveillance activities in public spaces. British civil liberties campaign think tank Big Brother Watch (BBW) supports the call. Silkie Carlo, director, said: “No other European country has a face surveillance epidemic like the UK, aligning us with the likes of China rather than our democratic counterparts. The public do not want to be walking ID cards, subjected to a constant police line-up. Tens of millions will have been scanned by facial-recognition cameras in this country, yet few know about it.”

articleTitle: Neurodivergents in tech ‘suffer more stress and discrimination’
abstract: A NEW STUDY focusing on workers in technology uncovered significant levels of stress and discrimination being felt among neurodivergent groups of workers — people with a set of diverse neurological conditions as a result of normal variations in the human genome, including autism, dyslexia and others — active in the technology sectors.

articleTitle: Airlines fall short in race to lower carbon emissions
abstract: AIRLINES ARE NOT doing enough to mitigate their carbon emissions and their impact on climate change, according to a study from the Transition Pathway Initiative (TPI), a group representing 40 investors with around $13tn in assets under management that assesses companies' preparedness for the transition to a low-carbon economy.

articleTitle: News briefing: R&D Huawei maintains tough strategy on patent protection
abstract: AMID EASING political pressure in the US, increasing appetite to cash in on its intellectual property (IP) and an aggressive legal strategy, an analysis by E&T and IFI CLAIMS shows that there is no end to Huawei's global R&D hegemony. Never touching below 8 per cent growth in US patent grants for 17 years, 2019 is likely to be another strong year for Huawei's global patent push in the USA — seemingly undisturbed by bad PR and US sanctions. This is revealed in projections by IFI CLAIMS, a patent service and leading provider of patent data.

articleTitle: The measure of beijing daxing international airport
abstract: On 25 September 2019, a few days before the 70th anniversary of the founding of the People's Republic of China, Beijing Daxing International Airport (PKX) opened its doors to passengers.
