abstract: According to Andreev, the project blends futuristic design principles with a touch of minimalist charm, providing an immaculate space for the revitalization of “Malta's tenacious spirit”

articleTitle: After all: Our columnist discovers a thriving Swiss industry, all but unknown outside Switzerland
abstract: IN ONE OF my latest ‘View from Vitalia’ blogs (bit.ly/eandtvitalia), I promised to tell you the story of a recent discovery of mine — that of Swiss wines and the technologies of their making. What better time to do so than in the run-up to Christmas and New Year when we start stocking up our wine cellars in preparation (mine lives on top of the fridge and is better known as the wine rack)?

articleTitle: Money + markets: Financial systems in countries like China, Japan and US support engineering and technology companies but in the UK, it's a different story. The UK markets just don't recognise their value
abstract: ENGINEERS DO NOT find it easy to prosper in the UK. The markets have historically had a love-hate relationship with them and the sort of systemic support they would get in Germany is simply not there in the UK. This is not much better for technology companies; most are scorned in the City and there are scant examples of them when you compare the scene with the US.

articleTitle: The final countdown: Here's a cheerful question: How do you think the world will end? Will underground monsters rise against us? Perhaps a giant asteroid will obliterate our planet? Maybe a nuclear winter will make survival impossible? All fun scenarios. This is our list of 13 (unlucky for some) possibilities
abstract: The 1974 book ‘The Jupiter Effect’ by John Gribbin and Stephen Plagemann foresaw that the end of the world would come from the alignment of the solar system planets. This would create many catastrophes, such as a giant earthquake on the San Andreas fault, which would occur on 10 March 1982. The best-selling book was wrong, but the future is always uncertain. Perhaps they were off by a few decades?

articleTitle: Money + markets: Without AI regulation, we're all at the mercy of the chronic algo-holics
abstract: TO BE A functioning member of a modern society is to be highly regulated. There are hundreds of thousands of pages outlining what is okay for us to do and what actions will get us fined or thrown into gaol. Markets are driven by a ‘winner takes all’ logic, and companies are lured by this logic too. Regulators set boundaries on acceptable behaviour in order to protect the common good. Of course they do.

articleTitle: Huawei ban sends stark warning on partnership
abstract: IN JUST A couple of days after the order went out from the White House to put Huawei on the US ‘entities list’, effectively banning the company from purchasing any products the US deems to be technologically sensitive, announcements by two companies — Arm and Google — indicated the precarious nature of an industry that relies on cross-border cooperation.

articleTitle: View from brussels: The outcome of the EU job shuffle will decide the direction of policy
abstract: BRUSSELS PLAYED host to the start of the Tour de France in July, but the annual cycle event is not the only fierce contest to have graced the Belgian capital recently. The race to fill the EU's top jobs is also in full swing.

articleTitle: Book interview: A novel approach to chemical engineering
abstract: "MY BOOK IS ABOUT someone who blows things up to keep people safe," says Fiona Erskine. Because her debut novel, ‘The Chemical Detective’, is a thriller, there can be no plot-spoilers here. But what can be revealed is that the heroine, Dr Jaqueline ‘Jaq’ Silver, like her creator, is a chemical engineer. To be precise, she is an explosives expert working in avalanche prevention. In the course of her routine work, she uncovers ‘something suspicious’ and ends up following a trail of clues to Chernobyl, where she discovers ‘something nasty’, the existence of which is masked by residual fallout radioactivity. If you want to know anything more about the narrative, you'll have to read the book, an activity that is highly recommended.

articleTitle: Big project, big delay? All over the world, engineering megaprojects run late and costs soar — but why does this happen and what can be done to prevent it?
abstract: IT ALL SHOULD have been so different. After nine years of construction work on Crossrail, 9 December 2018 was supposed to mark the beginning of passenger services on the most important section of the new Elizabeth Line railway, the underground tunnel linking Paddington in the west of London with Abbey Wood in the east.

articleTitle: World news
abstract: Australia's power grid has suffered outages after record-breaking heatwaves and surging use of air conditioners left power plants struggling to meet demand.

articleTitle: UK carbon footprint exports will intensify under natural gas boom: Ramping up the UK's liquefied natural gas (LNG) imports could mean indirectly shifting the responsibility of gas-related methane emissions to other countries
abstract: BRITAIN's AIM of setting itself apart with its ambitious zero-carbon target by 2050 is commendable. Yet, there remains reason to be critical. By importing liquefied natural gas (LNG) via global shipping routes and asking for climate-harming methane leaks upstream in the production chain, Britain and other countries add emissions to the greenhouse gas balance with little awareness. As LNG in Britain continues to boom, its heavy emission footprint is expected to complicate the debate over a greener economy.

articleTitle: Bletchley veterans hear how early computers helped plan D-day
abstract: NEW ARCHIVE research has revealed how German High Command messages decoded at Bletchley Park confirmed that an Allied deception operation had successfully fooled the enemy about the D-Day landing plans.

articleTitle: View from Washington: We often look to national programmes to support technology, but current US-China tensions suggest they no longer work
abstract: HOW MANY OF US have bemoaned Britain's apparent inability to draft and implement plausible large-scale technology policy? Well, as the US and China push ahead with separate national AI plans and, more recently, Washington has added a Quantum Economic Development Consortium (QED-C), continuing tensions between two superpowers have exposed major flaws in such programmes.

articleTitle: Who is programming whom? ‘I Am Mother’ provokes interesting questions about how human a non-human can be
abstract: THE DAY AFTER the human race becomes extinct a droid (known as ‘Mother’) selects a human embryo and grows it, within a day, to be a healthy screaming baby girl. It then nurtures this child (‘Daughter’) through to young womanhood, fulfilling all the necessary maternal duties along the way.

articleTitle: Book reviews: Because Internet, human/machine, every breath you take
abstract: INTERNET WRITING can be a bit of a joke. It is often used as lazy shorthand to mock young people as uneducated and unrefined, although I suspect it would be a struggle to find a 17-year-old who sincerely writes predominantly in emoji and ‘text speak’. Here, Gretchen McCulloch makes a convincing and lively argument that internet writing is a creative and natural extension of language.

articleTitle: Money + markets: Blockchain isn't just a new technology, it is a political disrupter that takes away the state's monopoly on money. try as they might, governments won't be able to legislate it away
abstract: ONE THING about technology in the modern world is that you can't uninvent it. Cryptocurrency is a genie out of the bottle and it is about to enter a new phase of expansion. While the price has been flying up and, as I write, down, this has been because of geopolitics: Iran and the US/China trade war. Where gold would have gone through the roof in the old days, the new go-to asset for the fearful is bitcoin. Gold did manage a good rally, but the technology of the blockchain is fast augmenting the ‘barbarous’ metal as ‘get out of dodge’ money. In a world full of societies like Venezuela and Iran, situations like Hong Kong's protests, and rolling trade trolling, the current highly regulated and penned-in financial system is desperate for liquid channels like cryptocurrency.

articleTitle: Money+markets: It's technology, not politics, that creates the feel-good factor
abstract: YOU CAN BE forgiven for being confused when trying to guess the future of the UK and world economy and therefore the direction of travel for the markets. There is no shame in that; a state of confusion is the aggregate state of investors, hence the day to day grind of volatility which is a solid measure of uncertainty.

articleTitle: Online privacy: Nearly all councils use marketing trackers on their websites
abstract: IN COLLABORATION with the Danish privacy and analytics company Cybot, E&T ran an analysis on 408 council websites in England and Wales and found that 96 per cent deploy marketing trackers and cookies, and many without the users' knowledge.

articleTitle: Photo essay: Plastic recycling workspace
abstract: PRECIOUS Plastic is a global network of hundreds of people taking a do-it-yourself approach to tackling plastic pollution by setting up shared workspaces where they turn waste into new products.

articleTitle: The measure of volvo concept wheel loader zeux
abstract: The Volvo Concept Wheel Loader Zeux is a digital protype for a real-world autonomous and fully-electric construction machine that first came about in 2016 at an informal team-building event for children.

articleTitle: After all: A historic German transport link that remains forever Belgian
abstract: IN MY PREVIOUS After All column I mentioned Vennbahn — a now-defunct Belgian railway that used to form several small pockets of Germany inside Belgium. Well aware of E&T readers' unfading interest in railways, I was not surprised to receive a number of queries about Vennbahn which I will try to address here.

articleTitle: The eccentric engineer: Introducing the machines that built the machines
abstract: IN THIS COLUMN we often talk about what engineers invent. Inventing can be a great way to make a name for yourself and can bring instant recognition. We all know Stephenson built the ‘Rocket’, but who built the machines that built the ‘Rocket’? What about all those engineers who make that inventing possible? Mechanical engineers need tools to build with, but inventing tools just somehow lacks the glamour of inventing ‘things’. So it's time to celebrate the engineers’ engineer.

articleTitle: Thinking cap: The circumference of the earth, probability and bank accounts are among this month's puzzles, with a prize to one winner
abstract: Alfred, a surveyor, found a long, straight canal, with no locks between two bridges exactly eight kilometres apart. Its water was perfectly still.

articleTitle: Interview ben saunders: World record-breaking ‘adventure style’ polar explorer, Ben Saunders discusses how a century of technology innovation has — in some ways — made today's expeditions easier than those of the ‘heroic age of exploration’, while in others, has made no difference
abstract: “IT WAS A tough camping trip,” says Ben Saunders. He's describing his 105-day Scott Expedition, the longest human-powered polar journey in history, in which the 41-year-old Briton and his travelling companion, Tara L'Herperniere, “suffered like dogs”. Coming from the third man to ski solo to the North Pole, who in the past decade has skied almost 4,000km in the Polar Regions, this is something of an admission. One of the expedition's aims was to complete the task that had narrowly defeated Captain Robert Falcon Scott of the Royal Navy in 1912: getting to 90-degrees south on foot… and getting back alive to tell the tale.

articleTitle: Pulling diversity together
abstract: Society does not change quickly. Entrenched views can take decades to overturn, sometimes requiring the changing of the guard to a more enlightened generation before true impartiality can be embedded — and even then it is clear that bias has a long and durable tail. But we are heading in the right direction.

articleTitle: 2020: Forecasts from the past: With 2020 just round the corner, we turn the clock back to revisit 20 technology predictions made about our future and ask if past predictors really had 2020 vision
The graphic: Cyber threat to European elections
abstract: European political institutions are shoring up their defences after predictably being targeted by Russian state-sponsored hackers ahead of elections in May to choose hundreds of new MEPs.

articleTitle: Photo essay: Sir John Alcock and Arthur Whitten brown were pioneering aviators, making the first non-stop transatlantic flight and transporting the first transatlantic airmail to Britain
abstract: TWO YOUNG RAF officers, Captain John Alcock (1892–1919) and Lieutenant Arthur Whitten Brown (1886–1948), made the first nonstop transatlantic flight on 14–15 June 1919, using a Vickers-Vimy biplane. They also carried several items of mail with them and, in doing so, effectively transported the first transatlantic airmail to Britain.

articleTitle: Interview Mike Wilson
abstract: “THE UK IS A long way behind in terms of productivity;" says Mike Wilson of the British Automation and Robot Association (BARA). "The increased use of robotics is an important element of addressing that shortfall." Wilson is the chairman of BARA, an organisation that represents "the supply chain for robot and automation products into the UK". Its membership consists largely of robot suppliers; systems integrators and component suppliers. BARA also engages with the academic community "principally in the industrial robot sector. Our main interests are manufacturing robots for manufacturing; as opposed to humanoid robots or robots in medicine."

articleTitle: Book interview
abstract: "ENGINEERING PLAYS a central role in civilisation," says Lord Browne. Always has, always will. "Without the tools and techniques created by engineering, the world would be a very empty, cold place. We wouldn't have energy. We wouldn't have mechanisms to enhance our memory. We wouldn't have the ability to keep ourselves safe. Engineering is essential, and the foundation of how we live."

articleTitle: In search of Greener seas: The results of the 2019 IET Global Challenge have been announced, with two inspiring projects winning the accolades
abstract: WERE Samuel Taylor Coleridge able to update his ‘Rime of the Ancient Mariner’, he might have changed its most famous line to: “Water, water everywhere, nor any drop without plastic contamination.” For in the 185 years since he wrote the poem, the challenge is no longer how to survive the seas, but is how the seas are to survive, given the rubbish we put in them. Apart from climate change itself, it is arguably the most pressing and high-profile environmental issue facing the world at the moment. It is timely, therefore, that the 2019 IET Global Challenge focused on this issue.

articleTitle: Gamers real world
abstract: E&T: How are you expanding your clients from games developers to design engineering and other new markets? Brett Bibby: “Anybody who is a pioneer that wants real-time 3D has been using our tools for a long time, so I don't know that Unity is moving there as much as it's being more widely adopted.

articleTitle: Education: Children's love for STEM on the decline, IET survey finds
abstract: A SURVEY AND series of interviews conducted by the IET has found that growing pressures in formal education are having a serious impact on school students’ perceptions of STEM subjects.

articleTitle: Thinking cap
abstract: The cardinal called on the master mason to discuss design of a mosaic floor, to be made near the altar of the new church being built. "To honour the Holy Trinity, we shall use an equilateral triangle, subdivided into many smaller equilateral triangles, in black and white tiles," said the cardinal, who believed that mathematics was one of the paths to God.

articleTitle: Big screen Gemini Man: Clone alone or are you alone when you have your cloned self chasing you down?
abstract: FILMS INVOLVING people being hunted down are nothing new. The hunters are typically out for bounty or revenge, or perhaps part of some sinister governmental or corporate plot. Of course they could also be aliens, robots from the future, dinosaurs — it's a long list. What sets ‘Gemini Man’ apart, though, is that the person who is hunting down Henry Brogan (Will Smith) is in fact himself (also played by Will Smith).

articleTitle: The bigger picture: Lazareth LMV 496
abstract: Dubbed ‘La Moto Volante’, French custom-automotive manufacturer Lazareth's LMV 496 is claimed to be the first motorcycle in the world that can transform into a quadricopter. "It's a flying motorcycle for real," according to designer Ludovic Lazareth, who says it takes about a minute to switch from electric-powered road bike to the four kerosene turbines that enable flying mode. So far, it's only been shown hovering in mid-air while tethered to a platform, but will reportedly be on show at the Gitex electronics trade show in Dubai in October. Pre-order prices are expected to be in the region of €496,000.

articleTitle: Book Interview: Greenland is rapidly becoming one of the world's most important science laboratories. Author Jon Gertner explains how this vast wilderness could hold the key to our understanding of climate change
abstract: ANYONE FOLLOWING the mainstream news in recent months will have come to realise that, when it comes to global warming, climate change and sea-level rise, there's a story that won't go away. Greenland's ice, according to one news source, is under a ‘death sentence’. While it's tempting to think this is typical of headline writer hyperbole, the old axiom of there being no smoke without fire holds true. Jon Gertner, author of ‘The Ice at the End of the World’, agrees that, despite hysteria levels in the press, the problem facing our ice sheets is serious.

articleTitle: The graphic: Stop and search under scrutiny
abstract: In the past year alone, two major UK think tanks have warned of the issues resulting from feeding racially biased data to UK police crime prediction models. One of the data types that experts find problematic is stop and search records. This dataset lends itself nicely to training AI models, but Big Brother Watch argues that even when ethnicity is omitted, other variables such as postcode can act as proxies to reinstate bias.

articleTitle: Buzz words
abstract: If you're afraid of the deep blue, this may not be for you… A UK-based immersive virtual-reality entertainment business, Immotion Group, has released a live-action VR experience, providing a rare glimpse and insight into one of the most mysterious creatures on the planet, the humpback whale.

articleTitle: View from Brussels: When you wish upon an EU star… departments vie for commission cash
abstract: EVERY FIVE YEARS, a new executive branch takes over the EU policy-making baton and continues the work of the previous commission, or decides to chart a course for its own priorities. That time is now. Since a new President-in-waiting, German foreign minister Ursula von der Leyen, was given the nod to take the reins this November, the commission's ‘civil service’ has been looking at how her administration should proceed in its first 100 days.

articleTitle: World news
abstract: A Chinese lander has safely touched down on the far side of the Moon in a historic first for space exploration. The Chang'e-4 probe communicates with Earth via a relay satellite.

articleTitle: View from Seoul: Bitter memories underlie expected memory shortages
abstract: DISPLAYS ON THE train from Incheon Airport to central Seoul usually tug your coat by promoting the South Korean capital's tourist traps. Nowadays, passengers get something else: a lecture about a centuries-old territorial dispute with Japan over an island cluster (Dodko to the Koreans, Takeshima to the Japanese). Growing diplomatic tensions could soon tear as serious a rupture in the global engineering supply chain as the Sino-US trade war.

articleTitle: The measure of InSight Mars lander
abstract: When InSight successfully touched down on Mars on 26 November 2018 it was the first lander to do so in six years. It was launched from Vandenberg Air Force Base in California on 5 May 2018.

articleTitle: Book interview: We've known the story of Apollo 11 for half a century. But in his new book on how humankind conquered the Moon, author David Whitehouse goes in search of first-hand accounts of one of the greatest tales ever told
abstract: FOR DAVID Whitehouse, “Apollo 11 is one of the preeminent achievements of humankind”. So much so that the author of ‘Apollo 11: The Inside Story’ predicts that in ten thousand years, when historians are describing the defining achievements of the 20th century, they “might mention the uncapping of nuclear energy or the unravelling of DNA. But above those, they will write of the first humans to walk on the Moon. Children will still listen to the words of Neil Armstrong as he stepped out of the Lunar Module. We don't have the words of Christopher Columbus. But those words of Armstrong will be with us forever.”

articleTitle: The measure of peregrine lander: The first American spacecraft expected to land on the Moon in almost 50 years will be an unmanned robotic lander built by astrobotic technology which will be launched by united launch alliance's (ULA) Vulcan Centaur rocket in 2021
abstract: Pittsburgh-based robotics business Astrobotics was selected to deliver up to 14 Nasa payloads to the Moon on its Peregrine lunar lander after taking part in Nasa's Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) programme, where nine companies developed small space vehicles and other technology for 20 missions to explore the lunar surface over the next decade.

articleTitle: Bizarre tech
abstract: I get the gimmick — global warming being shown by warming a mug, cute — but has this really been thought through? To get a hot beverage, you're going to probably employ a kettle, which uses electricity. This is quite likely to come from fossil fuels, unless you have your own little solar farm hooked up to your house and not the grid. Or 1,000 hamsters which power your home by running on exercise wheels.

articleTitle: A history of science in 20 objects
abstract: Beginning in Mesopotamia around 10,000 BC, previously nomadic tribes of hunter-gatherers began to settle and form agricultural communities. The age of agriculture spurred the development of new and increasingly specialised tools, like this Sumerian sickle, which dates back to 3,000 BC. One of many such tools recovered from the region, this instrument was probably used for agricultural and manufacturing tasks, such as gathering resources for food and construction.

articleTitle: Tech toys teach coding and drone piloting skills
abstract: THE TOY FAIR 2019 played host to a range of STEM learning toys as well as toys incorporating emerging technologies such as drones and mixed reality, helping children to learn technical skills at ever younger ages.

articleTitle: View from Brussels: Après Brexit, le déluge… EU summit finds its flood of ideas dammed
abstract: TWO YEARS AGO, when this meeting was planned, it seemed like a good idea for Europe's remaining premiers to put their heads together and dream up some policies to talk about before the end-of-month EU elections.

articleTitle: Buzz words: From a voice-controlled banker to a ‘virtual catwalk’, here are stories that make words like ‘artificial intelligence’ and ‘virtual reality’ trend
abstract: To all of you who like to do your clothes shopping online, this may be of interest. Online fashion and cosmetic retailer Asos has launched an augmented-reality (AR) experience within its app. ‘Virtual Catwalk’ enables users to see 100 new-in products at the click of a smartphone.

articleTitle: The graphic: Flight of the Crew Dragon
abstract: Crew Dragon is a passenger version of SpaceX's Dragon cargo ship. In its first mission, carrying a dummy astronaut, it successfully docked with the International Space Station on 3 March. The reusable capsule is built to last for 10 flights.

articleTitle: After all: How the spark gap proved itself mightier than the bomb
abstract: LAST MONTH, I was asked to give a talk on the enclaves of Western Europe at the Royal Geographical Society's London headquarters in Kensington. Enclaves have been one of my subjects of interest for years, but I was genuinely surprised by the sheer number of people who turned up to listen to the talk on such a relatively esoteric topic.

articleTitle: Book reviews: Beyond the Valley, Britain and the bomb, this is not propaganda
abstract: Published to coincide with the 50th anniversary of the internet (on 29 October 1969, the first message was sent between two computers connected on the ARPANET network), ‘Beyond the Valley: How Innovators Around the World are Overcoming Inequalities and Shaping the Technology of Tomorrow’ charts a course for a more balanced and less unhinged internet, and looks at how this could parlay into a broader social revolution.

articleTitle: The bigger picture: High-rise rescue net
abstract: Net Guard has been designed by a team of students in Guangzhou, China, as an example of how drone technology could be applied for search and rescue, especially in places that humans cannot physically reach.

articleTitle: The graphic: Patents reveal iPhone evolution
abstract: With critics bemoaning Apple's lack of innovation, and iPhone sales flagging, the tech giant is under increasing pressure to give its flagship device a radical overhaul. Newly filed patents hint at what's to come.

articleTitle: View from Washington: Have Silicon Valley's big beasts lost the power of the pivot?
abstract: "HEY GUYS, I just had a thought. So, this is it. A lot of successful start-ups launched with a different business model and when they ran into trouble, they pivoted to something new. Like Instagram — that was a location-based check-in service when they started and then they pivoted. Or Chatroulette — that was social media and then they pivoted to become a playground for the sexually monstrous."

articleTitle: The measure of mars helicopter scout (MHS): Nasa's mars helicopter — the first vehicle that will demonstrate the viability of heavier-than-air vehicles on another planet — has successfully passed rigorous tests of its readiness to travel with the Mars 2020 rover mission
abstract: KNOWN AS THE Mars Helicopter Scout (MHS), the drone helicopter was developed by Nasa's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) and Caltech, who have been exploring the potential of sending an airborne scout robot to accompany the Mars 2020 rover since 2013.

articleTitle: After all: Our columnist recalls his visit to Liechtenstein — the world's richest country: A financial powerhouse and ‘mini-industrial giant’
abstract: READERS OF After All might have noticed that the last three columns were all, to a certain degree, devoted to Europe's small geopolitical entities: enclaves, micronations and ministates, all prosperous and technologically advanced, despite (or maybe because of) their minuscule size.

articleTitle: The accuracy of Asimov
abstract: RUSSIAN-BORN Isaac Asimov was one of the most celebrated science-fiction authors in the world and wrote and edited over 500 books. Globally famous novels including ‘I, Robot’, ‘Nightfall’ and ‘Foundation’ were all penned by the prolific and successful forward thinker.

articleTitle: Wrong toys or the right play?
abstract: BY THE TIME we get to ‘Toy Story 4’, Andy's toys, including Woody and Buzz, are now in the possession of Bonnie (a family friend). But while Bonnie loves her toys, she introduces a new character, Forky — a spork endowed with goggly eyes and pipe cleaner arms — which has severe hang-ups about being a toy What is interesting, for this month's Big Screen, at least, is that Forky was made by Bonnie's own fair hand. Is a toy more loved because it has been self-made? Or does it suffer from longevity issues because, let's be honest, it's a bit rubbish. Forky; in the right of the main picture, is undoubtedly a bit rubbish.

articleTitle: The graphic man-made climate change: In various areas and regions in the world, we see the impact of global warming. With the help of open-source satellite images, E&T can show the effects of man-made climate change
abstract: After 16-year-old Greta Thunberg delivered a heartbreaking speech at the recent UN climate summit in New York, she became subject to the mockery of US President Donald Trump. Mere words and statistics may leave some people cold.

articleTitle: Da Vinci brought drawings to life
abstract: Part of Leonardo's genius lies in the fusion between engineering and art. To have that imagination and combine it with both mechanical understanding and the ability to create meaningful — and beautiful — drawings has inspired engineers for the last half millennium. Some of his inventions were deemed impossible, while many inspired real and recognisable objects that are part of our daily lives, albeit requiring modern materials and technology to make them workable. Here we look at a selection of Leonardo's drawings and real-life versions created from them.

articleTitle: 3D scanning will allow Heathrow passengers to keep liquids in carry-on luggage
abstract: PASSENGERS travelling through security at Heathrow Airport may soon be able to keep their liquids and laptops in their cabin bags thanks to the rollout of new 3D-scanning technology that can produce more detailed images than today's equipment.

articleTitle: View from Taipei: Taiwan demonstrates energetic response to ‘interesting times’
abstract: A FORMER TUTOR proposed that the Chinese curse, "May you live in interesting times" only worked if you added, "and not know it". Think about it: wishing such conditions on others implies you will suffer too. He also felt free to adapt it because there is no evidence anyone Chinese coined it — research traces its first use to a 1930s British politician.

articleTitle: Thinking cap
abstract: Farmer Brown and Farmer Jones had an angry dispute over the inheritance of two rectangular fields of the same size. Their case came before the King, who (supposing himself as wise as Solomon) gave judgment: “Farmer Brown will, with one straight line, divide the first field into two parts of whatever sizes he wishes,” said the King.

articleTitle: The bigger picture safer cycle helmet
abstract: Swedish company Hövding has released its third-generation cycling helmet with an airbag inside the collar. The result of four years of R&D, this model is easier to use, adjustable in size and incorporates Bluetooth, making it “the world's safest”, according to Hövding CEO Frederik Carling. Battery life is up to 15 hours, and the linked app shows time remaining and distance cycled. When activated, the helmet registers movements 200 times a second. In an accident, the airbag inflates in 0.1s to enclose the head and support the neck, and the app texts the location to an emergency contact.

articleTitle: Who saw that coming? I did!
abstract: In 1940, Robert Heinlein wrote a short story called ‘Solution Unsatisfactory’, in which the US creates a nuclear weapon before everyone else, becoming the only superpower, and everyone else gives chase to try and develop their own bomb. This is a carbon copy of the events of the nuclear arms race and the Cold War, which began after the US launched nuclear weapons against Japan in 1945.

articleTitle: View from Brussels: Infinity and beyond: EU space ambitions have a down-to-earth purpose
abstract: THE EU FLAG features 12 yellow stars, and the Union is increasingly shooting for their celestial counterparts, harbouring big dreams to punch above its weight in the global space race.

articleTitle: The bigger picture: Raffles city Chongqing
abstract: A megastructure featuring the world's highest skybridge has been structurally completed in China.

articleTitle: News briefing: Education Chinese tech scholarships used to bait Western students
abstract: An E&T analysis shows how China's technical universities ramped up scholarships to attract foreign students, as the mood between China and the US deteriorates further. FROM THE OUTSIDE, Chinese people living in China may be undisturbed by the increasing political tension between their nation and other superpowers, notably the US. However, early signs suggest a shift in the higher education sector of both countries, possibly connected to the present political turmoil.

articleTitle: Interview Carsten Welsch
abstract: “WHEN MOST PEOPLE hear the term ‘particle accelerator’, the one machine they think about is the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at Cern, because it is the biggest atom smasher in the world,” says Professor Carsten Welsch. Yet what is far less well known “is just how many particle accelerators there are in the world and what applications they're used for”. Welsch estimates that globally there are probably somewhere in the region of 50,000 accelerators in operation, of which only a “tiny fraction” are at all comparable in size to the LHC, the biggest machine in the world.

articleTitle: Book interview: New light on Tesla's electrical future
abstract: “WHAT INTERESTS ME about Tesla,” says Iwan Rhys Morus, “is the way he portrays himself as inventing the future.” Idolised by the current generation of tech entrepreneurs — he's even got an electric car named after him — Nikola Tesla is today's blueprint for how the 21st century is inventing itself in its own image. But Tesla himself — widely accepted as one of the great engineering minds of the late 19th and early 20th century — is a challenge to any biographer. Running in parallel with his legendary achievements is a compelling personal narrative of a complex character manipulating his own image.

articleTitle: The graphic potential for reducing carbon emissions: Britain's commitment to a net-zero carbon economy by 2050 raises the stakes for large businesses. But an analysis shows that efforts could be rewarded
abstract: MUCH OF THE carbon emissions debate is increasingly obsessed with firms and their actions to become carbon-clean. Public awareness in consumption is reflecting this trend. More consumers are demanding that firms become active in reducing the carbon footprint of their products. How much carbon dioxide corporations should be allowed to blow into the air will increasingly be on the agenda of regulators.

articleTitle: The eccentric engineer: The highs and lows of America's first black female pilot
abstract: TO SAY Bessie Coleman was born into deprivation would be an understatement. Her parents were sharecroppers in late 19th-century Texas, picking cotton and taking in laundry to get by, and she was the 12th of 13 children. Bessie's father was Native American Cherokee while her mother was African American, so almost every door to improvement was closed to them. Not that this put her off.

articleTitle: Buzz words: From faking smiles to smelling like lemons post-workout, here's what makes words like ‘artificial intelligence’ and ‘wearables’ tick in our brains
abstract: Smiles at the ready! Or not… You can never truly tell if a person's smile is genuine or not. So, to try and tell a real or fake smile apart, researchers at the University of Bradford have developed computer software that can spot false facial expressions.

articleTitle: Photo essay: Open access to elite training
abstract: Cyclists have real-time test data projected onto the floor in front of them so that any changes in position or performance can immediately be seen. Four HD cameras catch all angles.

articleTitle: The gallery
abstract: In the robotics yard at Nasa's Jet Propulsion Laboratory is the prototype of the transforming robot, Shapeshifter. Made of smaller robots that can morph into rolling spheres, flying drones, swimming submersibles and more, the concept robot is a step forward in the search for aliens.

articleTitle: Back to former Glory
abstract: "LEONARDO WAS A great fiddler," explains Professor Martin Kemp, an expert on the artist at Oxford University. "He almost always found it hard to settle on a single composition and would often change his mind." We know this, in large part thanks to the emergence of highly sophisticated tools that use infrared light to peer beneath the surface of the master's works.

articleTitle: The bigger picture: Adidas Futurecraft loop
abstract: A decade of research by sports brand Adidas and partners across the world has gone into the company's first trainers that can be completely remade into a new pair of high-performance running shoes when they wear out. Unlike typical sports footwear, which includes complex mixes of materials that make recycling difficult, the Futurecraft Loop range is made from reusable TPU (thermoplastic polyurethane) that is spun into a yarn, knitted, moulded and fused to a midsole without the use of glue. Once the shoes come to the end of their initial life they can be returned to adidas to be washed, ground to pellets and melted into material to make a new pair with zero waste and nothing thrown away. First-generation designs are being beta-tested by 200 users ahead of wider release to the public planned for 2021.

articleTitle: View from Washington: The 2019 UK General Election is set to import new, more hidden, digital campaigning technologies from the USA
abstract: K STREET IN Washington is the historical home of the political lobbying and campaigning industry. As the UK advances towards December's general election, its leading players are watching closely.

articleTitle: The measure of Duracell battery elephant
abstract: Battery manufacturing company Duracell, collaborating with artist and sculptor Tony Diaz, created this model to raise awareness of the 20,000 tonnes of portable cells ending up in landfill sites across the UK every year — the equivalent weight of around 4,000 elephants.

articleTitle: News briefing: World news
abstract: The CEO of Ethiopian Airlines says he "believes in Boeing" despite the crash of a 737 Max plane that killed 157 people and has been attributed to software failings.

articleTitle: Richest councils recycle much less: The most affluent councils in England have been found to recycle less of their household waste, a new E&T analysis reveals
abstract: BRITS LIVING IN AFFLUENT areas might be expected to recycle more. They may have the money, the education and potentially the awareness of environmental issues connected to household waste. But according to a new E&T analysis, the opposite is true.

articleTitle: Mixed reality is ‘third paradigm of computing’, Microsoft claims
abstract: A SENIOR Microsoft manager has suggested that immersive computing will be at the core of the next paradigm of computing.

articleTitle: TheBiggerPicture: Digit delivery robot
abstract: Ford is teaming up with a US robotics firm to automate delivery of parcels up to 18kg. Digit, a two-legged robot built by Agility Robotics, travels with its load in the back of a self-driving vehicle. At the destination it unfolds itself and carries the package to the customer's door, walking like a human to negotiate steps and uneven ground – obstacles that make wheeled robots unsuitable for home deliveries.

articleTitle: Disabled explorers reach new heights: No trail is too rough, no rapid too turbulent, or no mountain too high for a new generation of technology-assisted disabled adventurers
abstract: WE WERE climbing in the foothills of the mountains on the island of Tenerife. My climbing partner, my 25-year-old daughter, huffed and panted as we cut our way through the bushes, me lagging as she forged the path ahead. We stopped to admire the view below — a vast expanse of land, a tempting emptiness on this otherwise crowded island. Then we turned our eyes and aimed back upwards.

articleTitle: There's no place like home
abstract: THERE WAS A time when, for a film to count as a proper film, it needed to be aired at the cinema. This is largely Holywood sniffiness that hasn't recognised some great films made for TV — although dated, ITV's ‘The Long Good Friday’ remains one of my all-time favourites. However, the viral success of ‘Bird Box’ last year combined with the Oscar-winning recognition for ‘Roma’ has reinforced Netflix originals as part of the movie industry mix.

articleTitle: Book reviews: Six impossible things, energy at the end of the world, Tim Cook
abstract: "QUANTUM PHYSICS is strange." These are the first words of John Gribbin's brilliant new book, the title of which is taken from the University of Oxford mathematician Charles Lutwidge Dodgson's philosophical fiction. Dodgson is, of course, better known as Lewis Carroll and the book to which Gribbin refers is ‘Through the Looking Glass, and What Alice Found There’, in which the White Queen assures Alice that, in her youth, she was able to believe "six impossible things before breakfast".

articleTitle: Interview Suryansh Chandra: Co-founder and co-CEO of British desktop robot arm manufacturer Automata, former architect Suryansh Chandra is on a self-proclaimed mission to automate the world of small-batch manufacturing by ‘democratising robotics’
abstract: “THEY CANNOT compete with a human in terms of intelligence. They cannot compete with a human in terms of perception. But a robot is very good at doing a narrow set of things,” says Suryansh Chandra. “If you want to pick something up and put it somewhere, and you need to do that task 2,000 times a day, let a robot do it.”

articleTitle: Quantum: Get ready for hyperdrive!
abstract: SOME technologies have always been at a comfortable arm's length. Nuclear fusion, for example, has been 20 or 30 years away for at least 30 years. Other technologies have seemed equally futuristic but, like an autonomous car, could be arriving on the doorstep in the very near future. It is in this category that Quantum technologies fall.

articleTitle: Book Reviews: The artist in the machine, magnificent women, super pumped: The nature of computerised creativity, pioneering women who challenged the all-male world of engineering, and the remarkable story of Uber
abstract: As we all know, machines are getting smarter. They're also getting more creative. A robot equipped with sufficiently cutting-edge artificial intelligence and machine-learning technology can now behave in almost human-like fashion. It is that ‘almost’ that is one of the tenets of this book.

articleTitle: Thinking cap
abstract: A mouse starts a maze at A. Each time she comes to a junction, she chooses one of the available paths at random. When she reaches one of the three exits (B, C or D) the test is over. Only one exit (D) has cheese.

articleTitle: Which materials will shape the future?
abstract: MATERIALS HAVE defined the development of humankind from the first day when one of us cracked a nut with a stone. As we look back over that 2.5-million-year period, the rate of technological development during the three classic prehistoric ages of stone, bronze and iron was remarkably slow considering the inventiveness of the human brain. Perhaps innovation itself is a learned behaviour and it was only when the Middle Ages came to a close that minds were encouraged to be agile and creative. From this point, the acceleration of engineering was closely tied in with the emergence of engineering materials, and — as you will see in the following pages — substances such as glass, aluminium, steel and plastics became worthy of ‘Materials Ages’ of their own.

articleTitle: The Eccentric engineer: How sea sickness and near-suff ocation spoiled a romantic getaway
abstract: THE SEASON OF weddings and honeymoons is upon us and there can be few groups in society more romantic than engineers. So where would an engineer honeymoon? Cern? The Tacoma Narrows? Both have their positives, but few have had quite the impact of mining engineer Ben Carlin's suggestion to his new wife Elinore: "Let's spend our honeymoon crossing the Atlantic in a Jeep."

articleTitle: Sci-fi wise guys: Can science-fiction authors see the future? And just how accurate are they? Here are some of the best predictions — some of them may surprise you
abstract: One of the best sci-fi novels of all time, ‘1984’ highlights many issues we seem to have in our society now.

articleTitle: No-deal Brexit could affect UK autonomous vehicle plans
abstract: A NO-DEAL BREXIT could have a significant impact on the anticipated benefits of the autonomous vehicle industry, experts say. Calculations for inbound investments were made on the basis of a favourable Brexit and not on a no-deal scenario. With the latter now likely, it came as a surprise when a newly launched roadmap paid no heed to any Brexit scenario. The new ‘UK Connected and Automated Mobility Roadmap to 2030’ report, produced by Zenzic, outlines more than 500 milestones on how to get autonomous vehicles onto the road in the next decade.

articleTitle: Thinking cap
abstract: Leonardo da Vinci sketched many inventions, among them a parachute on a page devoted to different forms of flight in the ‘Codex Atlanticus’. He made this sketch in 1485, although the modern parachute was not invented until the late 18th century (in 1783, Louis-Sebastien Lenormand jumped from the observatory in Montpelier).

articleTitle: The measure of Solar Voyager
abstract: THE SOLAR VOYAGER is an electric vehicle which is fully powered by solar energy and created with 3D-printed parts made from recycled plastic. It featured as part of an expedition to the South Pole.

articleTitle: She cannae take it, captain: At the heart of many a good science-fiction tale you will find space ships that can travel across the Galaxy. Could this ever happen?
abstract: ANY SPACE ADVENTURE that goes beyond the Moon or Mars inevitably trips up when it comes to the practicalities of travel. Quite often the most satisfactory explanations are those which don't really mean anything. For ‘Star Trek’, dilithium crystals just did the job and without further examination we were motoring along at warp factor 2.

articleTitle: World news
abstract: An alleged drone sighting temporarily disrupted flights at Dubai International Airport, which is the world's busiest for international travel.

articleTitle: Thinking cap: This month's puzzles are inspired by cats, cubes, codes and cold-blooded creatures
abstract: Joe had been given a join-the-dots drawing book for his birthday. Joining the 68 black dots shown, he made a picture of a cat. “I wonder how big it is,” Joe said, and proceeded to mark with an orange dot each point of the grid inside the outline of the cat. He drew 93 orange dots, as shown.

articleTitle: Interview Emily Penn
abstract: “BECAUSE WE LIVE ON LAND, it's easy to overlook problems the world's oceans face,” says Emily Penn. “I've seen enough science on this to show me that people need to change their attitudes to plastic in the sea. But at the same time, I'm aware that when you try to solve something and you don't really know where to start, the best solution can be hard to find.”

articleTitle: Book interview: Is there anybody out there?
abstract: THE FIRST PROBLEM facing anyone seriously considering the question of whether there is life elsewhere in the universe is to reach an understanding of what the concept of ‘life’ might mean. Without that we can't prepare ourselves for the implications of whatever answers our scientific investigations may return. It's an issue Andrew May is happy to address in his new book ‘Astrobiology: The Search for Life Elsewhere in the Universe’, but it's one that, even when expressed as a pair of simple alternatives, immediately seems to take us away from what we're all secretly hoping for: the universe of ‘Star Wars’ and ‘Star Trek’.

articleTitle: UK's first rocket returning home after half a century
abstract: THE UK'S FIRST and only rocket to successfully launch a satellite into orbit has finally been returned home almost 50 years after it came down to Earth in South Australia.

articleTitle: The bigger picture: Hyundai Elevate walking car
abstract: SOUTH KOREAN carmaker Hyundai has revealed a concept electric vehicle that has not only wheels but also robotic legs, enabling it to travel in even the most challenging environments. Unveiled at this year’s CES technology show in Las Vegas, the Elevate concept is designed to help emergency workers move across harsh terrain in the event of a natural disaster, but could also be used in more mundane situations such ‘walking’ right up to a wheelchair user’s front door.

articleTitle: Foldable screens and 5G compatibility steal the show at MWC
abstract: FOLDABLE DEVICES mark the "biggest change" ever in the smartphone industry according to Huawei's mobile boss Richard Yu as he unveiled the company's Mate X foldable smartphone at the recent Mobile World Congress in Barcelona. The device came just days after Samsung announced its first foldable phone, the Galaxy Fold.

articleTitle: Bizarre tech
abstract: I… I kind of love this? Normally this sort of thing would give me creepy vibes. But I kind of want LOVOT to be my pet. Or my child.

articleTitle: This is the age of the digital twin
abstract: ORIGINALLY, THE BIRTH of the digital twin stemmed from the design process which, apart from where design spins off to art or hand-crafted creations, is a digital process. Obviously this has transformed design and manufacturing, and it has consequently become more accurate, repeatable and reusable. Automation within the process has smoothed the flow through design, prototyping, ramp-up and full manufacturing. But just when you might think the impact of digital technologies was reaching its limit, designers, manufacturers and operators started to realise that further opportunities were presenting themselves. And so the concept of the digital twin emerged.

articleTitle: Maney+ markets: Monetary policy turns the unorthodox into the ordinary
abstract: THERE ISN'T MUCH engineering and technology done these days without rivers of capital being diverted into the balance sheets of companies involved. US corporate bonds alone account for $8 trillion of debt.

articleTitle: High life in a black hole
abstract: ‘HIGH LIFE’ DOESN'T FEEL like a science-fiction story, in as much as the science fiction forms only the backdrop rather than troubling the actual storyline too much. Instead, it is a drama based around a group of predominantly young adults that find themselves thrown into long-term coexistence in the confines of a space ship.

articleTitle: After all: Sharing a joke and a hotel room with inspector Clouseau
abstract: IN A TRUE WHODUNIT style, we begin with a corpse in a hotel room. Or rather with the coffin containing the dead body of a hotel guest, who — after a thorough investigation by detectives — turns out to be alive, albeit fast asleep, and even snoring loudly!

articleTitle: There is still time to ‘save our seas’!
abstract: WHILE THE CONSEQUENCES of plastic pollution are becoming obvious, so are the causes. Eighty per cent of marine litter originates from land, with only 9 per cent of plastic currently being recycled globally. Every year, somewhere in the region of 12 million tonnes of plastic enters the oceans. Single-use plastic and cigarette butts are the biggest threat to oceans and marine life.

articleTitle: Book reviews: The next billion users, future histories, manual for survival
abstract: The next wave of digital media adoption will come from the three billion people on the planet who live on less than two dollars a day. These are the global poor. They live in India, Africa and China, among other places, and their lives will be transformed as they embrace social media, internet research resources and mobile telecommunications.

articleTitle: What to do with pandemic flu: The UK government has designed a contingency plan in the event that a deadly disease wreaks havoc on the world. But what needs to be done if, or when, the time comes?
abstract: IF YOU HAD TO SUM UP the national sentiment towards flu in a single word, you'd be pushed to do better than ‘glib’. Flu isn't serious. Not serious-serious. It's in the sweet-spot: serious enough to avoid a dreadful wedding no questions asked; not so serious that you're expected to spend those days bedridden or hospitalised. In 2015, a study by healthcare provider Benenden of 2,500 UK employers and employees found that ‘flu’ was the third most popular excuse for missing work after vomiting and diarrhoea. That's flu, to us in the UK: food poisoning, but a bit more dignified.

articleTitle: Buzz words
abstract: We live in a world where some individuals like to access data and tamper with it. Such tampering with data is a definite no-no in trials for pharmaceutical drugs. Why? Because changing results in pharmaceutical trials could make a treatment look more effective or could diminish the side effects of a certain drug.

articleTitle: Bizarre tech
abstract: This isn't just any pillow. This is a Nanu pillow. To the naked eye, it looks like a seemingly standard piece of bedding. However, the Nanu is supposed to give you the perfect night's sleep. How? Because it now knows everything about you. Like a bunny boiler ex-girlfriend.

articleTitle: After all: Italian ‘Bedfordino’ community built up brick by brick
abstract: READERS OF THIS column may be aware of my ever-growing collection of geopolitical curiosities: enclaves, micro-nations, mini-states etc, all of which have featured on this page.

articleTitle: News briefing: How article 13 could threaten smaller content providers and start-ups
abstract: THE EU PARLIAMENT has voted in favour of Article 13, establishing new rules for copyright on the web. However, some experts have argued that smaller content providers could be hurt by the new rules.

articleTitle: Interview Jamie Stapleton
abstract: "WHAT WE ARE doing is creating a step-change in digitalisation, and part of that is to change the conversation with the customer," says Jamie Stapleton, digital leader in the transformers business of ABB's Power Grids division, part of the $4bn global engineering giant that focuses on "hardware-software services solutions delivered to clients requiring power grid infrastructure". With more than 200,000 projects completed in the sector, ABB can, with some justification, make the claim to be a leader in the production, monitoring and maintenance of transformers. Yet, with ubiquitous industrial digitalisation, times are changing, and the way transformers are starting to be delivered as integrated digital systems is putting a new complexion on an industry where it is common to find 50-year-old units still operational in the field. Advances in digitalisation mean the way transformers are inspected is changing too.

articleTitle: BOOK interview: The rails to victory
abstract: "FROM AN engineering point of view it was the railway workshops that became a major part of the war effort," says Anthony Lambert, railway historian and transport expert.

articleTitle: View from Brussels: EU plots new industrial revolution with ‘battery alliance’
abstract: AMID ALL THE Brexit white noise at last month's European Council summit, one little nugget nestled among the leaders' conclusions that escaped the scrutiny of most backstop and no-deal aficionados.

articleTitle: View from Washington: Silicon Valley's natives are uncommonly restless
abstract: SILICON VALLEY is not known for staff protests. Its companies claim to offer good salaries, excellent working conditions and the chance to ‘make a difference’.

articleTitle: Buzz words
abstract: As of 2017, 40 per cent of women and 18 per cent of men have experienced unwanted sexual behaviour in the workplace.

articleTitle: Money + markets: Universal basic income: Not so revolutionary
abstract: TECHNOLOGY IS GOING to make us all unemployed, so they say. AI and robots are going to make us all obsolete, jobless and therefore starving. Even engineers and technologists will be replaced by mighty computing devices that will do a better job than the bald monkeys who created them.

articleTitle: Big screen the wandering earth: The wandering earth
abstract: NEVER MIND AI, ‘The Wandering Earth’ shows China matching the US in another high-profile part of the global economy, the Hollywood blockbuster The year's biggest box office hit so far, it has earned more than £500m since Chinese New Year, and become the latest slice of slick Mandarin multiplex movie-making to grab international attention.

articleTitle: Book interview: Reinventing technology from scratch
abstract: THE PREMISE is literally fantastic. Ryan North's latest book posits a hypothetical situation in which your FC3000 model time machine has malfunctioned. You find yourself projected back in time to a world without technology. Unable to repair your FC3000, you need to invent some of the basics, and you need to invent them fast. You do, however, have one advantage: and that is you know what it is you want to invent. You see, you already know of the existence of the integrated circuit and the internal combustion engine, the pendulum and the bicycle. It's just that you've taken them for granted, and while you've been happy as your future self to use them all, you have no idea how they came about or indeed, how to set about creating them for yourself. ‘How to Invent Everything’ is a time-traveller's manual that will bring you up to speed. And in the best tradition of sustained literary spoofs, Ryan North didn't so much write the book as find it.

articleTitle: Editor's letter
abstract: FOR A TERM that right now sits at the very top of the Gartner Hype Cycle the digital twin idea deserves to be better known than it is. Gartner places the digital twin in the digitalised ecosystems trend alongside better known technologies like blockchain and the Internet of Things, but it has certainly not yet entered public awareness in the same way as buzzwords like artificial intelligence, driverless cars or even quantum computing.

articleTitle: Buzz words
abstract: A new method developed by researchers at RMIT University in Australia has mastered the complex Atari video game, learning from mistakes and identifying sub-goals 10 times faster than Google DeepMind to finish the game.

articleTitle: The eccentric engineer: James Graham: A wannabe electrical engineer and doctor
abstract: IN THE EARLY DAYS of any subject, it can be hard to tell science from snake-oil.

articleTitle: Quantum for dummies: The basics explained
abstract: Every particle, atom and molecule [photons, electrons or whole atoms] behave in accordance with the laws of quantum mechanics — as does everything. However, this only becomes important when broken down to the atomic, sub-atomic and molecular scales. Quantum mechanics is trying to use the physics of things at the atomic level to create effects in the macroscopic world — which is our world.

articleTitle: Book reviews: Team human, a bright future, the life, science and times of lev
abstract: One of the biggest problems confronting those responsible for formulating public policy on climate change is not so much that the public dislikes climate change, but that it dislikes the voices it hears discussing it. On the right hand of political debate you have denial, alongside the advocacy of industrial progress at all costs, while on the left you have self-promoting environmentalists who can seem puritanical and at odds with economic development. The centre can only muster up suggestions for small-scale energy generation which, while genuinely having a greener future at heart, are mere drops in the ocean in terms of the global problem.

articleTitle: Social media firms told to protect children
abstract: CONCERNS ABOUT social media aggravating poor youth mental health have been reignited following the death of Molly Russell, 14, whose social media feeds were reportedly filled with distressing content. Molly's father said that he has "no doubt that Instagram helped kill my daughter".

articleTitle: Japanese spacecraft touches down on speeding asteroid
abstract: A JAPANESE spacecraft successfully touched down on a speeding asteroid last month as part of a mission to collect samples that could provide clues to the origin of the solar system and life on Earth.

articleTitle: Brain-computer interface tech scoops inaugural E&T innovation prize
abstract: A non-invasive neurotechnology platform that uses artificial intelligence to translate brainwaves into control signals was named as the first winner of a new E&T-backed prize for Innovation of the Year at the IET's 2018 Innovation Awards in central London.

articleTitle: Money + market: Money drains away and markets crash — but they will rise again
abstract: THE UNITED KINGDOM'S stock market is down on its luck and is falling heavily Brexit is a disaster, you might say So why wouldn't the UK stock market crash? But global markets are crumbling too, and the reasons are not glaringly obvious.

articleTitle: Economic fears stalk the chip business
abstract: MALCOLM PENN, president of market analyst firm Future Horizons, has for many years characterised the wild oscillations of the semiconductor market as being under the influence of the "four horsemen". If they all falter, a massive slump looms. If they ride together, the industry can look forward to boom times as it did in 2017 and 2018. This year, one in particular looks quite unhealthy, but the others are still cantering well.

articleTitle: View from Brussels: Uncertainty means post-Brexit aviation is up in the air
abstract: THE GULF STATES have been a thorn in the side of European air carriers for some time now. Legacy airlines like Lufthansa, Air France-KLM and British Airways have seen their lunch gradually eaten up by the likes of Etihad and Qatar Airways.

articleTitle: Thinking cap
abstract: Many years in the future, a mission of humans discovers a far distant planet, now abandoned, but once inhabited by a non-human advanced civilisation. As they explore the planet, the mission realises, from the wealth of strange artefacts discovered, that the alien civilisation used technologies almost incomprehensible to us.

articleTitle: View from Washington: Grandee Kissinger raises spectre of an AI arms race
abstract: HOW DO YOU control arms whose capabilities must, by their very nature, remain secret?

articleTitle: News analysis: Design for a trust-free environment
abstract: THE RECENT opening in Brussels of what Chinese telecom giant Huawei calls its Cyber Security Transparency Centre is the latest in a series of attempts to stop its equipment from being banned from lucrative 5G and other large-scale telecom contracts. It will probably be as successful as the others: doing little to assuage concern while providing a highly publicised indication of the looming problems that face not just Huawei but any firm making computers and communications gear in a world where capitalism and nationalism are set on a collision course.

articleTitle: Most innovative designs at iF design award 2019
abstract: SINCE 1954, the iF Design Awards have been recognised as an arbiter of quality for exceptional design. Now, 65 years on, they are among the most prestigious design awards in the world. On 15 March, this year's winners were announced in a ceremony at BMW Welt in Munich.

articleTitle: Book interview: A demon in the works
abstract: "JAMES CLERK MAXWELL'S is a lovely story about someone that's not well known to the general public. Maxwell should be up there with Newton and Einstein," says Brian Clegg, author of a superb new biography of one of the greatest scientists of the 19th or any other century For Clegg, the reason Maxwell should be better known is simply that the work conducted by the Victorian scientist laid the foundations for what could be achieved in 20th-century physics.

articleTitle: Editor's letter
abstract: TECHNOLOGY SOMETIMES feels like the new Wild West of the modern world: full of exciting opportunities but also dangers, a lawless place that does things by its own rules or no rules at all. That's not necessarily a bad thing — just an inevitable consequence, for a while at least, of its pace of change.

articleTitle: Let's dismantle the idea of male and female brains
abstract: Gina Rippon: The ‘whack-a-mole’ myth is that there is such a thing as a male brain and a female brain, where the male and female refer to a brain from a man and a brain from a woman. The idea is that the biology or biological programming which determines the anatomical characteristics of a man and a woman also determine brain characteristics has been around for 200 years or more, where scientists work backwards from a kind of political status quo where women were socially, educationally, financially and politically inferior and they took it upon themselves to believe that could be explained in terms of brain characteristics. Down the years, there's been a kind of ‘hunt the differences’. People would say they had found the explanation and then somebody else would say "No, that methodology doesn't work" and it keeps coming up. It's a perpetual idea.

articleTitle: Thinking cap
abstract: The Corvidians were an intelligent alien race evolved from bird-like creatures. Their technology had developed differently from that of humans, due to their aerial and arboreal environment. When humans invented the wheel, the Corvidians invented the parachute. Most Corvidians were compulsive gamblers, with a passion for bright, shiny jewels and metals. They would bet on anything, such as when a parachute would reach the forest canopy, or which leaf would first fall from a tree. Their scholars had developed probability and statistics ahead of other branches of mathematics.

articleTitle: View from Brussels: French and German giants fail to railroad the EU into relaxing rules
abstract: FRANCE'S ALSTOM and Germany's Siemens had their commercial hearts set on a merger of their rail businesses that they said was necessary to make sure foreign companies, particularly those from China, do not steal a march on Europe's train builders. Ministers from both countries were also in favour of pooling resources.

articleTitle: The eccentric engineer: The enduring relic of an imperial capital that was never built
abstract: IF THERE'S ONE thing that megalomaniacs tend to have in common, it's a love of grandiose statements. Hence, behind every tyrant, there's usually an ambitious architect. Behind them, a very nervous structural engineer.

articleTitle: Photo essay
abstract: We all remember the music video from the legendary Michael Jackson's hit ‘Billie Jean’, with the pavement illuminating when the King of Pop stepped on each slab. Well, that's what a group of researchers from the University of Pavia in Italy have created.

articleTitle: Help us record our tech history
abstract: WALKING TO THE IET'S London offices from Embankment Tube Station, it is easy to overlook an old-timey-looking street lantern at the bottom of Carting Lane, directly opposite the stage door of the Savoy Theatre.

articleTitle: Big screen Alita: Battle Angel: Part Angel, Part demon. Part human?
abstract: I'M NOT GONNA lie, as the young people say — there are loopholes in ‘Alita: Battle Angel’. The sort of loopholes that the engineering mind is better switching off from if it is to enjoy the film. For instance, given that we are fairly confident that there is currently no meaningful life on Mars, how did it manage to evolve into a civilisation of such sophistication by the 23rd century that it was able to send an invasion force to Earth? Or that one of the Martian space ships should come to life 300 years after crashing into a swamp? Or even that Alita, a devastating tornado of a cyborg, should be dumped into the trash when her abilities, and presumably therefore her value, are so immense. However, I switched off from the loopholes, and did thoroughly enjoy the film.

articleTitle: Book reviews: Robot rules, monitored, shoot for the moon
abstract: TV's ‘Big Brother’ is about to mark the 20th anniversary of its 1999 birth in the Netherlands. In the UK, where it enjoyed some of the greatest popularity of all its international versions after the first series in 2000, it hasn't even made it to two decades, ending quietly — for now, at least — at the tail end of 2018.

articleTitle: They built this city on rock and roll
abstract: HUMANS WERE ALL but wiped out in the 60-minute war — we blasted ourselves into oblivion with "a terrible flurry of orbit-to-earth atomics and tailored-virus bombs". A couple of millennia (although the timeline is vague) down the line and America is still a wasteland. But elsewhere life survived and we now live in the Traction Era — the dystopian backdrop to ‘Mortal Engines’.

articleTitle: Why Europe's roads are not yet swarming with electric cars
abstract: IN THE EARLY hours of 11 April, European leaders helped Britain slam its foot on the brake pedal and delay its exit from the EU until Halloween night in October. But unlike the protracted Brexit wrangling, the switch to electro-mobility is gradually making progress.

articleTitle: The Eccentric engineer: A tale of two countries and two clever chemical engineers
abstract: ALUMINIUM is one of the most useful metallic elements for engineers, being light, strong and self-protected in its metal form by a quickly formed layer of oxide. Yet for most of human history it has been rare and precious, simply because it was enormously difficult to isolate.

articleTitle: Interview Matt Brown
abstract: "FOR ALL THE TECHNOLOGY we have around us, the whole point of the process is to tell a good story " Matt Brown is taking me on a tour of London's Imaginarium Studios, which creates computer-generated performance motion-capture for film, games and, more recently, mixed reality If you've seen any of the ‘Lord of the Rings’ movies and are familiar with the character of Gollum, played by Andy Serkis, you already know what ‘mocap’ is. If you've seen Serkis's performance as Caesar in the recent ‘Planet of the Apes’ franchise, you'll know how far it's come. "Andy's performance as Caesar is completely driven by performance capture," says Brown, "and that's the sort of work we typically do here."

articleTitle: Bizarre tech
abstract: This slightly satanic robot is 25cm of pure nightmare fuel. The Elfkin, which looks like it would suck your soul out with one glance, is dubbed ‘your child's first social network’. It takes recorded messages that you send through the app, and plays them.

articleTitle: Book reviews: Not all dead white men, playing smart, on the future
abstract: The world is changing so fast that Martin Rees is probably justified in revisiting the same territory he covered in the 2003 book that he wanted to call ‘Our Final Century?’. As he admits, his UK publisher persuaded him to remove the question mark, while US readers got ‘Our Final Hour’.

articleTitle: How to build the quantum Internet
abstract: COMPUTERS AND THE internet have revolutionised our lives, having both a profoundly positive but also, oftentimes, negative impact on society Yet, it's impossible to imagine life today without the World Wide Web.

articleTitle: Book interview: Where now for chemistry?
abstract: "I DIDN'T WANT to write a simple history of chemistry in the 20th century," says Bernie Bulkin. "I believe we engage people by telling stories. That's what makes us human beings." Bulkin is discussing his latest book, ‘Solving Chemistry: A Scientist's Journey’: in effect part biography of the discipline of chemistry and part autobiography of a chemist, both presented through tales of the problems he worked on as a professional chemist.

articleTitle: The eccentric engineer: Lift off! How the elevator shaft came before the elevator
abstract: NOT ALL GREAT engineering inventions come out of the blue. Sometimes it seems inevitable that a ‘thing’ will be invented soon and those with foresight can prepare for it. That's just what industrialist Peter Cooper was doing when he built his Cooper Union for the Advancement of Science — now one of the USA's leading engineering colleges.

articleTitle: After all: Climb on board the self-operating ‘Shabbat elevator’!
abstract: ONE OF THE most disturbing sites I saw in South Korea was Dorasan train station on the Seoul-Pyongyang line, built during the temporary thaw in North-South relations, the so-called Sunshine Policy, under North Korea's previous leader Kim Jong Il, right on the troublesome North-South border.

articleTitle: Interview Sir Peter Knight
abstract: "WE LIVE IN A quantum world," says quantum physicist Sir Peter Knight. "We don't often exploit it, but there are examples where we do. The semiconductor is a quantum thing, without which we wouldn't have classical computing chips." He adds that the first quantum revolution, which started almost a century ago, "has transformed our world". Today we are seeing the second, which "hinges on a really weird property of quantum physics in which you can put quantum systems into more than one state at the same time".

articleTitle: After all: Long live the glorious space Kingdom of Asgardia!
abstract: WHAT? YOU'VE never heard of Molossia and Freedonia? How about Liberland, Seborga or Asgardia? Well, I don't blame you if you haven't, for all of the above — and several dozen others — constitute one of the most obscure areas of modern geopolitics, the so-called ‘micronations’ (not to be confused with ‘mini-states’ such as San Marino, Liechtenstein etc). Each of them, according to Wikipedia, is "an entity that claims to be an independent nation or state but is not recognised by world governments or major international organisations".

articleTitle: View from Brussels: Will Brussels match climate hot air with positive action?
abstract: IF 2018 SHOWED anything, aside from that satire is dead, it's that climate change, plus policies that influence it, are in the spotlight more than ever before.

articleTitle: Reviews interview: Let's stand up for ‘team human’
abstract: Douglas Rushhoff: We're using digital technology in order to try to automate human behaviour. The more people think or the more individual people are, the more anomalous behaviour we have, the harder it is to predict our behaviour and lump us into statistical buckets. We're currently using digital technology — mainly algorithms and sorting procedures — to limit human choice.

articleTitle: The graphic: Scientific achievements of 2018
abstract: JULY: Astronomers using the Very Long Baseline Array (VLBA) system of 10 radio telescopes discover the brightest object in our universe. The quasar, named P352-15, is 13 billion light-years away from Earth and started when the cosmos was less than one billion years old — just 7 per cent of its age today.

articleTitle: View from Washington: AI enters the ethical minefield, but who is holding the map?
abstract: ETHICS ARE POISED to overtake innovation in dictating the rollout of artificial intelligence (AI) - and sideline the US's and UK's roles in its regulation. Two of the world's three biggest digital markets, the EU and China, aim to solidify AI ethics policies over the course of the year, with barely disguised social and economic intent.

articleTitle: Money + markets: Smoke-and-mirror money: The incredible vanishing companies
abstract: HOW IS IT that a company like Carillion, with 43,000 employees, can go bust and vanish overnight? How can a listed company with millions of audited profit and cash in the bank, like a recent retail bakery, suddenly collapse with a massive overdraft and huge losses? How can a financial system or a market support entities with such complex activities whose existence or otherwise is catastrophically binary?

articleTitle: Scottish factory converts plastic waste into road paving material
abstract: PLASTIC WASTE is to be used to pave British roads in the future thanks to a new factory in Scotland.

articleTitle: View from Washington: There may be trouble ahead… are we ready to face the music?
abstract: AS SOBERING thoughts go, the fact that a possible no-deal Brexit only limps in at the bottom of global economists' Top 5 concerns for 2019, if at all, is a quadruple espresso.

articleTitle: The online world: 2018
abstract: Nominet has released the third edition of its alternative online map of the world, in which countries are scaled according to the number of internet domains registered to their local country code top level domain (ccTLD). The 2018 map is based on the 153.2 million domain names that use country codes — up from 143.6 million in 2017.

articleTitle: Bizarre tech
abstract: You should never leave dogs in cars, hot or not. Almost imperceptible temperature changes in the vehicle can kill your pooch.
